speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Is he in a position to make a report on the disastrous fire on the Vancouver waterfront yesterday? speechtext:

1546	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry and last evening the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) spoke to me about the subject matter.
I have before me a wire which gives the general situation, in so far as it can be ascertained at this time, and perhaps I might be allowed to read it to the house:
A serious fire broke out at about 11.45 a.m., yesterday, in Vancouver, destroying jetty No. 3 and loading galleries serving elevator of the United Grain Growers Limited as well as their warehouse on Burrard inlet. The adjacent warehouse, belonging to Buckerfields Limited, containing feed'grain and fertilizer, was damaged. The fire was reported under control at 2.45 p.m. The United Grain Growers Limited expect to continue operations by using Kerr Gifford elevator, which is not busy at the present time.
Elevator No. 3, leased to the United Grain Growers Association of Canada, is the property of the national harbours board. It is estimated the damage, together with all other damage suffered by the national harbours board, amounts to from $1 million to $1,500,000. The elevator is covered by insurance to the extent of $1,949,000, with loss payable to the national harbours board. Over and above this there was some damage suffered to the property of the Canadian National Railways. Five box cars were destroyed. One other box car was completely destroyed on an adjacent elevator track, and two* other box cars were damaged, but they can be repaired.
The position in so far as shipping is concerned is that the shipping in the harbour is not interfered with in the slightest, with the exception of course of the jetty and pier at which the fire took place. From there shipping has been prohibited. The national harbours board began yesterday the conduct of an investigation into the cause of the fire, but it will be some days before a report is available.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the appointment of a special committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not be a member of this committee; therefore I wish to refer to a matter which on several occasions over the years I have brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), and to which reference was made yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I refer to Canadian National Railways pensions, and in particular to the basic pension payable under regulations, not only those existing since 1935 but also those now in effect following the recent changes in connection with pensions in general.
As a result of the recent announcements, considerable improvement has been effected in respect of those in the service who are on pension and who made contributions thereto. But there is no improvement whatsoever in respect of pensioners who did not or will not make contributions.
I wish to refer briefly to the summary sent out by the chairman and president of Canadian National Railways on March 8 last, directed to retired officers and employees receiving pensions under the rules of the Canadian National Railways pension plan, and in particular to that part of the summary which deals with existing pensioners and makes reference to the revisions described therein. I might say that in general the revisions are very satisfactory, and the president and officers of the railways and the chairmen of the various brotherhoods who co-operated in arriving at the pension plan, one very much in keeping with that in effect in the United States, deserve commendation.
At the moment I am raising no objection to the general plan. I believe it is a step forward, one that was necessary and one which, for the last four or five years I have been recommending,-a pension plan in keeping with the responsibilities of those engaged in transport, and one that is actuarially sound.


One of the great difficulties in connection with the plan is that it does nothing for pensioners who are at present on pension. The part of the letter to which I have made reference states:
The foregoing revisions are applicable to those in the service at January 1, 1952, and who had not attained age 65 prior thereto.
And then it says:
A pensioner who did not contribute during his service towards a supplementary annuity will continue to receive the basic or service pension to which he is entitled under the existing rules.
That, I submit, is quite unjustified. The amount payable as basic pension is $25 a month. It is an amount that is not reasonable, satisfactory or justifiable. A great many of the employees of the railway company did not make contributions. The contributory feature did not come into effect until 1935. The numbers were set forth in Hansard on March 12, 1951, in answer to certain questions asked. The first question was:
How many retired employees of the Canadian National Railways are in receipt of pensions of less than $25 per month?
The answer was that there were 24, under the C.N.R. prior plan. Then the next question:
How many are in receipt of only the basic pension of $25 per month?
The reply was that there were 3,256. Then the next question was, in part:
How many are in receipt of non-contributory service pensions (a) $25.01 to $29.99 per month; (b) $30 to $39.99 per month; (c) $40 to $49.99 per month?
The answer was:
(a) $25.01 to $29.99 per month, 745; (b) $30.00 to $39.99 per month, 670;	(c)	$40.00 to $49.99 per
month, 330.
In other words a great many of these retired employees are today in receipt of basic pensions that are not in keeping with a national organization such as the Canadian National Railways. After all, if the government goes into business it should at least pay pensions that would be in keeping with those paid by private industry.
In addition to the questions asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, there was a further series of questions as to how many were in receipt of pensions from $25 to $30 a month who had made contributions. The answer was that there were 459. Of those receiving between $30 and $40 a month who had made contributions, there were 2,115. In other words, out of some 105,000 employees, of whom some 40,000 are contributors, there is a goodly number who receive a pension which has not been improved in recent years and whose claims have

been ignored as a result of the findings and conclusions of the committee set up for the purpose of deciding the matter.
Therefore, the responsibility for those who are pensioned rests directly upon the Department of Transport. I am sure that the minister is most sympathetic toward the request made by these people, but sympathy alone is of little use. Recently representations were made to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport by the Canadian Railway Pensioners Association, the grand president of which is Mr. J. T. Cormier, of Moncton. I am going to read the pertinent part of a submission that was made and ask the minister whether representations have been made to Mr. Gordon and the directors of the railway company to give consideration to increasing the amount of the basic pension to the end that a fair and a reasonable basic pension will be provided for those who are at present pensioned.
The pertinent part of the submission reads:
Whereas the Canadian National Railways are owned by the people of Canada and operated by a board of directors appointed by the hon. Minister of Transport on behalf of the government of this country, and whereas the government has from time to time assisted various groups of citizens through subsidies and other assistance, etc., we feel we are justified in requesting assistance for this group of railway pensioners, also due to present high cost of living and devaluation of our purchasing dollar, and knowing that a large number of railway pensioners are in distress, having to depend on charity and municipal assistance, we feel therefore that the present government should direct the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways to provide to all Canadian National Railways pensioners an increase of basic pensions, in order to afford a large number of pensioners a reasonable standard of living, seventy per cent of which do not benefit by old age assistance, under the age of seventy years, particularly retired railway pensioners who through physical disability brought on by hardships suffered in the course of their employment or through service in the defence of their country.
I realize that the minister may take the stand that it is not for him to direct the directors of the Canadian National Railways. Subject to his views in that regard, which I am sure are far removed from directing the directors of the Canadian National Railways, and deleting that portion of the representations, I suggest to him that a strong case has been made out by these people. Their number is considerable; the claims they make are definite, and the grounds for consideration reasonable.
It is not a case of asking for the expenditure of a large amount of money. It is simply a question of asking for assurance that former government employees shall be maintained on an equality with those who have served private industry. Certainly the present
24. 1952	1549
Committee on Railways and Shipping basic pension of $25 a month is not in keeping with the dignity of the individuals pensioned; nor is it, may I say with the greatest deference, in keeping with the dignity of this country.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and also the continuing plea that has been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on behalf of these Canadian National pensioners receiving $25 per month. I do not propose to go into the details, because this has been done by the hon. member who has just spoken, and who read to the house the submission made by these people.
I am interested in this matter because my home city is on the main line of the Canadian National Railways. Many people there are affected seriously by this limitation in pension, and many of them have approached me on the matter. I consider it my duty and a privilege to bring it to your attention.
It is true that changes have been made in the Canadian National pension scheme which have resulted in improvement for those now working, but I emphasize the word "now". It also improves the position of those who have been retired on pensions toward which they have contributed in part, that is, those who are receiving pensions of over $25 per month. But there is no improvement at all for those who are retired on pensions of $25 a month.
Of late consideration has been given in most pension schemes to the increased cost of living. Bonuses have been attached to many pensions and wage scales, and I do not see why the same thing should not be done for these people.
It is not clear to me whether this is the responsibility of the government or of the Canadian National Railways, but in view of the connection between the two bodies I am sure that if the government were to give the green light, Canadian National Railways could be persuaded to do something about it. I hope when the minister closes the debate he will answer the questions put to him yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to what progress has been made in considering this matter. Consideration of this matter was asked for some time ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in fact on March 20. At that time the minister said that he had assured the delegation which had approached him that the matter would receive consideration.
That was a month or so ago and I repeat the question my colleague asked yesterday:

Committee on Railways and Shipping What progress has been made in giving consideration to this group whose pensions are limited to $25 per month, an amount upon which it is impossible even to hope to live?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I feel that something more should be said with regard to these Canadian National pensioners. It is important to bear two things in mind. First, we are not discussing those who are now employed or those who have contributed over five per cent of their gross earnings during their period of employment.
I understand that both these groups will benefit under the new pension scheme, for which a good deal of credit should be given to the officers and directors of the railroad and the government. I am pleased to join with those who have expressed that view, but this new scheme does not benefit those already retired who in the past have not contributed more than five per cent of their earnings.
The other point which should be made clear is that although a committee is to be appointed to review the operations of the Canadian National Railways for the past year, there would be no point in discussing this matter in that committee. This is about the only place where we can usefully discuss the matter at this time.
My information is that at one time the officers of the railroad did recommend a scheme which would have benefited these retired employees about whom we are now talking. However, the tentative agreement, which would have been very beneficial and which was approved by the president and, I am given to understand, by the board of directors, was not approved by the government, in spite of the president's efforts to have it approved. If that be the case-and the minister can confirm whether or not it is -the situation is that there is not much point in our getting after the president of Canadian National Railways in the committee to do something which would benefit these pensioners because, depending upon how far he is able to go, his answer must be: Well, I have done all I can, and it is now up to the government. That will be the situation, because it appears that Mr. Gordon and the directors recommended a scheme which would benefit the men but Mr. Gordon was not able to have it approved by the government.
I do not think anything further need be said to emphasize the fact that $25 a month is not enough on which to live. I think nothing need be said as to the humanitarian aspects of the matter. Like the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am sure the


minister is as sympathetic to the plight of these men as anyone on this side of the house who has spoken about the matter or has taken an interest in it otherwise. But, as has been said, sympathy is not going to help people to live.
It seems to me that the only obstacle to acceding to the request can be the ground that it would involve an expense to the treasury. I should like the minister to confirm my understanding or point out that it is not correct. I understand that the request of these pensioners could be met without a direct grant by the government out of the general tax revenues of the country. The point that has been impressed upon me by the pensioners' association, who have'discussed the matter with me in the past, is that their position is that they have contributed in the past to the Canadian National Railways pension fund. They are not asking the government to make a grant so as to increase their pensions, but are asking that the increase be taken out of the C.N.R. pension fund. They say there would be a sufficient amount built up in the fund in future years to enable the request to be met without direct cost to the government.
They point out that they are the people who in past years did contribute to the fund, and although they did not contribute the maximum equal to five per cent of their earnings, they are amongst those who have built up the fund. They say that any increases in pension payments, even the increases now authorized under the new plan, will of necessity have to be taken from the present fund, and that even though increased contributions will be required in future from present employees, the fact is that increased payments to those who have contributed the maximum of five per cent will not come from anything further that they contribute. They say that in the case of an employee who is retired now and goes on pension immediately his increase will not come out of anything he has contributed over and above his former contribution, because there will not be time for the increased contribution to become effective.
They point out that the increased contributions mentioned by Mr. Gordon as justifying increased pensions to the limited class to which it would apply will not show any tangible return for the first five years, that there will be no tangible effect on the pension fund and that employees retired during that period will not have had an opportunity to contribute an amount sufficient to pay for

the increased pension payments they will now receive for life. In their representations they also have this to say:
To us it is inconceivable that an increase in pension payments will be made available in the future to seventy per cent of the employees who have to date contributed nothing to the fund while thirty per cent of the former employees who were regular contributors to the fund will not receive the Increase as stated by Mr. Gordon.
As I understand it, the injustice there is that, although these men have not contributed as much as five per cent, they have helped to build up the pension fund. Simply by virtue of the fact they did not contribute up to five per cent maximum they get no increased pension. On the other hand, an employee who retires the day after the new plan comes into effect, and whose contributions at the increased rate will not have had any effect on the amount of the pension fund, will get a pension at the increased rate. Their point is that they helped to build up the fund over the years and that they are now getting nothing extra from it, while the man who helped no more proportionately than they have is now going to get an extra payment from the fund. On the face of it I must say it seems difficult to me to describe that situation as anything but an injustice.
As I say, they make the additional point that they are not asking for a grant from the government or for anything that will increase taxes. They are asking that they be taken care of out of the pension fund which they helped to build up. They have made a submission which to me at least appears reasonable. They say that with the new scale of contributions they could be taken care of as requested out of the pension fund as it now stands and as it will be in the future without the necessity of a government grant.
I hope the minister will review the whole matter. There is no point in our taking it up again with Mr. Gordon before the committee, because I understand he has done his best, made his recommendation, and the present scheme is all he has been able to secure. It seems to me the matter rests entirely with the minister and the government. I hope the minister will have it reviewed and see if he can accede to the request of these $25 a month pensioners.

I wish to refer to the introduction of diesel-operated locomotives into the Atlantic division of Canadian National Railways. A few years ago in the committee there was an understanding that

If this plan is proceeded with, the most assured market for Nova Scotia coal will be destroyed. Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the house for this short and interesting debate on the subject of the pensions of employees of the Canadian National Railways. I am particularly pleased that the view of the house is that the position is far better than it was when the earlier debate took place, and of course with that I am in full agreement. That is one point the house perhaps should take into consideration, namely the improved pension position of C.N.R. employees, both those retired and those still on duty.
There are several points I would like to make, as briefly as possihle; but two in particular lead me to make the statement that the position of these men is far better than it was when the debate took place last year. The first of these points has been mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I believe by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who referred to the revised pension rules of the Canadian National Railways. There is no doubt that the pension plan has been greatly improved. I would remind the house that the revised rules were arrived at following discussion between officers and employees of the Canadian National Railways. After they had studied the matter for many months, if not more than a year, they recommended to the government the adoption of the new pension plan, which I believe is far better than the old one. It received the full approval of the men, and I believe there is correspondence on record to indicate that while the pension plan does not go nearly as far as many of us would like, it is nevertheless a great improvement over the previous plan.
That is the first point I wish to make, namely the substantial change in the position of these men. The next point is that this house approved a universal old age pension of $40 a month without a means test for those over 70 years of age, the total cost being met by this government. It also passed legislation providing for a pension of $40 a month, half the cost to be paid by this government, to those between 65 and 70, with a means test. As a result the man who is in receipt of a basic pension and who is 70 years of age gets an additional $40 a month, ac does the man between 65 and 70 who can prove his 

position to be such that he is in need of the additional amount. So the position in reference to these men is far better than when the matter was discussed earlier.
Another feature seems to have been forgotten entirely. It is that no official representations were made to me by the president or the directors of the Canadian National Railways along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton).

In the light of the legislation brought down in the house the whole position concerning the pension discussions, to which I referred a moment ago, with Mr. Gordon and his predecessor Mr. Vaughan, was reviewed not by us but by the pension committee of the Canadian National Railways in co-operation with their men. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 23, consideration of the motion of Hon.

Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in proceeding with this debate I should like to draw attention to a statement made the other evening in this house by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) when, as reported at page 1474 of Hansard, he said:
. . . there is not much satisfaction to many of our taxpayers to hear these millions and billions bandied about-they do not live in a world of millions and billions; they live in a world of fives and tens, and less than that. It Is the ordinary taxpayer that I am interested in, and it is the ordinary taxpayer that this house exists to protect.
I believe that this is a profound truth that is too often overlooked in this chamber. After all, we are here to provide for and to protect the interests of all the millions of little taxpayers in the whole of this dominion of Canada. As taxes rise and the basis for taxation becomes increasingly important, the deductions from income which are allowed before the incidence of tax become a matter of grave concern to every employed person and to every recipient of income from any source whatsoever. As the high levels of tax are maintained, and the prices at the consumer level increase or fluctuate in a tantalizing manner, as they do, around the peak, it becomes necessary to pay more and more attention to the alleviation of distress, particularly in the lower income brackets.
When I was preparing the notes from which I propose to speak today I was surprised to find that about 75 per cent of them dealt with income tax, and it may well be that in the time at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I may not be able to speak about anything but income tax. There are several matters that I should like to bring to the attention of this house, matters that have come to my attention possibly because of the peculiar nature of my own business. One is the matter of taxation of pensions; that is, privately purchased pensions, which should claim the attention of this house.
We assume that a man purchases a pension payable to himself on retirement or to his estate upon his demise. The pension was provided, let us say, by tax-free contributions, and therefore it is fully taxable as income when it is received. Well, that is all quite regular; it is an accepted fact, and the purchaser knows it before he makes his contract. The purchaser dies, and the widow is the sole beneficiary. The pension is then valued for succession duty purposes and is part of

the estate that he has left. So the duty is paid out of cash resources, with the result that the balance in the estate yields a reduced income. The widow is taxed duty on the estate, and income tax is payable on the revenue from what is left of the estate after the payment of that succession duty. It is, I submit, an anomaly that the value of the pension is fixed for succession duty without any abatement of income tax; because if the state removes say 25 per cent of the value as succession duty, then theoretically there is only 75 per cent left to provide income, and that 75 per cent of the income should be taxed; either that, or no income tax should be payable until the widow has received as much in pension as she had paid out in succession duty on the value of the pension. Certainly there is an element of double taxation in the present system, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the situation should be corrected.
The subject of double taxation brings up another point. Two years ago double taxation received the attention of the government, and a manner of relief was granted to the taxpayer, whereby he was permitted to deduct from his tax the amount of 10 per cent of the net dividends which had been received from taxable Canadian corporations. On the 1951 return it works out something like this. In order to illustrate the point I have calculated on a hypothetical income of $7,000, the whole of which was secured from dividends from taxable Canadian corporations. I have selected $7,000 and the status of a married person because, with the $2,000 exemption, it gives us a nice round figure of $5,000 on which to calculate. That may be a lazy woman's way of doing it, but nevertheless that is what I have done. I found out that that person will owe $1,104 in tax, composed of the regular income tax and the surtax on investment income. Added to this $1,104 in 1951 there was first of all the defence surtax of 10 per cent, which came to $110.40, and brought the total tax payable up to $1,214.40. Then, and only then did the 10 per cent of net dividends apply against the tax payable. Now the net result of that is this: Had the 10 per cent of net dividends been deducted from the tax payable, the total tax payable, before the imposition of the surcharge, the taxpayer would have benefited to the extent of the 10 per cent originally intended. However, now that the defence surtax has been added first, the taxpayer finds that instead of 10 per cent allowance for income from taxable Canadian corporations, he has a 9 per cent allowance.
As we go into another taxation year we find that the situation is worsened to this extent: Instead of the 10 per cent defence surcharge 55704-991
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough we have the 20 per cent surtax, and following the same procedure right down the line we find that we have the same tax at the level before the application of the defence surtax of $1,104; with the addition of the 20 per cent, it brings it up to $1,324.80, and on the $1,324.80 the $700 tax refund applies. Had the tax refund been taken off the total tax before the imposition of the 20 per cent defence tax, the taxpayer would have his full 10 per cent. As it is, if the government proceeds in this manner in 1952 as it has for 1951, the taxpayer will lose an additional 2 per cent, and instead of the 10 per cent allowance he will find that he has an 8 per cent allowance. This is in spite of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that the corporations did pay the defence tax; so the double taxation is indeed doubled and redoubled, let us say.
This relief was intended in the first instance as a straight deduction from total tax. I would just like to say this, and maybe I can pass it on as a word of advice to the minister. I hope he has already thought of it. Before he has the income tax returns printed for 1952 I hope they will be carefully reviewed. If this juggling was not deliberate, then the forms should be printed in such a way as to permit the deduction of 10 per cent of dividends from taxable Canadian corporations before the imposition of the defence surtax. If it was deliberate then I can only say one thing, namely, Indian giver.
It might also be noted that anyone who has investment income of over $2,400 is also liable for the 4 per cent surtax, which added on about 25 per cent or more to the net allowance of 10 per cent of dividends, so that the person who has followed the advice of the government from time to time and has been thrifty, has saved his money, and then, possibly being a bit of a gambler has invested in Canadian corporations, purchasing stocks which pay him dividends, and on which, as income of each company, the tax has already been collected-he has not invested his money in bonds-he has not invested it in real estate; he has invested it in industrial Canada. And because the government took cognizance of the fact that there was this element of double taxation, the relief was granted.
It would seem that, having granted that relief, the government has repented, and these people are in the position of being penalized for their thrift. Possibly it is a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul, but it seems to me it is a matter that should be considered carefully and rectified before the end of the present taxation year. I find it

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough hard to believe that this was done deliberately. I think the effect of such action must surely have been an oversight in the department.
There is also a recommendation with respect to this 10 per cent of dividend income which was passed on to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) by the taxation section of the Canadian Bar Association and the legislation committee of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants in March of 1952.
Among many other recommendations, all of which in my opinion are remarkably commendable, there is one that has reference to a situation obtaining where the spouse of a taxpayer has investment income which is not sufficient to warrant the payment of a tax. In other words, if I may quote from the recommendation:
The result Is that in many cases the supporting spouse pays a greater tax than would be exigible if his spouse's income in excess of $250 were in fact added to his own income. This will be true in every case in which the supported spouse's separate income over $250 is less than the aggregate of the tax exemptions to which he or she is entitled.
Then these organizations make this recommendation:
It is accordingly recommended that the act be appropriately amended so that in cases to which section 25 (2) would otherwise apply to supporting spouse may at his option and for all purposes of the act elect to have any specific items of the income of the supported spouse treated as his income and excluded in computing the income of the supported spouse.
This is a situation with which all accountants are familiar, and I trust the government will accept the recommendation of these two responsible bodies, and implement the recommendation.
I could not speak in this debate without touching upon a matter that has received considerable attention in the last few days, and one upon which I spoke when the resolution with reference to the elimination of the four per cent hold-back on medical expenses was being considered. At that time I cited a hypothetical case of a taxpayer who was supporting another individual who was ill and who eventually died. The taxpayer was not only burdened with this expense but, in addition, was reduced in status from the married to the single state. Peculiarly enough, on the very week end, when I went back to my office I had the exact duplicate of that case placed before me, upon which I was asked to prepare income tax returns.
I should like to place before the house the facts of that case. This woman had not been enjoying good health, and because of that her
[Mrs. Fairclough.1
income had suffered. She had not been able to devote to her business the attention it had formerly received. Her sister, who was dependent upon the taxpayer in question for support, and who had lived with the taxpayer for many years-indeed, I believe, all her life-became very ill.
When the taxpayer brought her income return to me and asked me to figure it out she placed before me medical bills which, upon totalled, showed the sum of $2,990.20. In addition to that there were $500 funeral expenses. Meantime the income of the taxpayer had shrunk to the point where she could claim only $107.60 of the medical expenses in computing her tax for 1951. She said to me, "What shall I do with the rest of these bills?" I said to her that I was sorry, but that so far as I could see she might as well forget she had ever paid them, because she could not claim a cent of them. This taxpayer could not understand why in 1952 she could not claim some of these bills. I believe her point was well taken, and that she should have been able to claim them. The fact is however that one can claim expenses only on behalf of a dependent, and the position then was that the taxpayer in question was no longer supporting the dependent. Therefore she could not claim, despite the fact that some of the bills were incurred in the latter part of the year and that, in normal circumstances, if her sister had lived she could have made the claim under the twelve months provision.
Had the sister lived, the taxpayer would have had not only the opportunity to claim for these bills but an additional exemption by reason of her having supported the sister. It is clear therefore that this taxpayer was placed in a peculiar position. As a woman past middle age, and one who had worked for many years, she had accumulated some small savings, the greater part of which have now been dissipated through the payment of these extraordinarily high medical expenses.
If the department has not already considered the matter, then I suggest to it that provision should be made for cases such as the one I have described, and that in the year following that in which the taxpayer has incurred the expense an opportunity should be afforded to deduct from taxable income those medical expenses paid out on behalf of a person deceased. I agree that this provision could not be extended over a period of years, but I believe an allowance might be made in the year immediately following. I commend this to the department for its consideration.
In connection with the elimination of the four per cent, I have worked out a few specimens which I believe the house will find

interesting. The first of these deals with a single person receiving a salary of $50 a week and who, as in. the case of the woman whose circumstances I have just described, was responsible for a dependent for whom heavy expenses were incurred. This person maintained the dependent in a self-contained: domestic establishment, and would be entitled to married status affording a tax exemption of $2,000. Then the taxpayer loses the dependent and is left with some heavy bills which, as obtained in respect of my client, could not be paid in one year. We will say that in the first year the taxpayer pays $300 or $400 of the bills which have accrued. He will then deduct from the amount he claims for medical expenses four per cent of his income of $2,600, or the sum of $104. If we suppose that he took off $400 he would have to deduct therefrom $104, leaving $296. As I mentioned before in the other case, the rest of the expenses that would have been paid in subsequent years could not be charged at all. This is slightly different from the other case I gave as an example. In this case the person could not pay all the expenses at once and they had to be spread over the years.
Many institutions and medical people in this country would probably just address their bills to the taxpayer and say "for professional services" and forget that the person on whose behalf the expenses had been incurred had died. In that way the taxpayer would be able to claim those expenditures as medical expenses. I do not like that way of doing things. . I think we should make provision for these -cases so that we do not force people to evade the law in order to obtain their just deserts. Even in such a case the taxpayer again loses out on the 4 per cent income in each year. If it takes three years to pay this he loses, as I said the other night, not 4 per cent but 12 per cent of his income in exemptions.
The next specimen which I worked out had to do with a married man with two children making $60 per week. With his exemptions his taxable income would be $820, which would put him in the lowest bracket of 15 per cent. He would pay 15 per cent on the $820 with the surtax of 20 per cent on top of that. That would cost him $147.60. Suppose he has $120 in medical expenses. The extra tax on the $120 at 18 per cent would be $21.60 which he would lose because the $120 would be short of the 4 per cent of his income and therefore he could not claim anything. Supposing that he has more than $120, he still loses the 18 per cent tax payable on the 4 per cent of his income, which is a difference of $22.46.

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough
Likewise the man who makes $75 a week, is married with three children. He would have a tax payable-I will skip all the preliminaries-of $271.80, counting the defence surtax. Supposing he had $450 in medical expenses, which is not even out of the way in many cases if you have but one serious illness in a family of five people; if the total were allowed, his saving would be $91.80. However, if the 4 per cent is disallowed then he saves only $59.98. In other words, by reason of this 4 per cent floor he loses $31.82 in taxes.
I maintain that this situation should be corrected. There are a great many families who, expenses being as they are, find it difficult to bring up children in the manner in which they would like to bring them up, or even to provide for them certain things which we in our modern age consider necessary. From the taxpayer's standpoint each year he is robbed of 4 per cent of income in the matter of this tax exemption. It is quite feasible that even with a small income that would mean $150 tax exemption in each year. If he is bringing up three children- take the case I mentioned of a $3,900 income -he loses a tax exemption of $156 each year because we must recognize that while every family would not have medical expenses, the average family with three children is apt to have medical expenses. It takes one form or another, either dental care, the youngsters getting measles or chickenpox, someone breaking a leg or having to go to the hospital for appendicitis or tonsillitis. All these things cost money. When you have even a minor operation you find that the bills run up.
I do not think it unreasonable to assume that a man in that tax bracket or that income bracket would have $150 medical expenses every year, but he cannot claim one cent because he has not yet reached 4 per cent of his income. Over a period of ten years while his family was growing up he would in fact lose $1,500 in tax exemptions. A saving in tax exemption of that size might mean all the difference between university or no university for one of the children.
When the parliamentary assistant was speaking yesterday he made a statement to which I must take objection.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Greenwood says "only one?" I must admit that he made a great many, but I do take great exception to one statement. On page 1524 of Hansard he is reported as having made this statement:
In this instance, if the four per cent, which is less than the national average of hospital, medical, dental and drug care, was removed, that would
1558	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough remove four per cent of the present taxable income of this nation. It would result in a reduction in our personal income tax receipts of four per cent or approximately $48 million.
I do not understand how the parliamentary assistant could make a statement like that. Such a figure must be predicated on two assumptions. First, that the personal taxable income is $1,200 million, and second that every taxpayer would have medical expenses up to or exceeding 4 per cent of his taxable income. That is just sheer nonsense. The white paper tabled when the minister made his budget speech gave a preliminary estimate of personal income taxes for 1951 as $890 million, and I find this figure in table 4 on page 13. I assume that that is the calendar year. Then on page 78 where they deal with the last five fiscal years the tax revenue from individual income tax is estimated at $980 million.
Upon asking a question of the department I secured a figure for the actual individual income tax receipts of $975,776,000. Even that amount does not come anywhere near the supposed $1,200 million upon which the parliamentary assistant's statement would have to be figured. As I said before, it would have to be predicated on the assumption that every taxpayer in the country would have medical expenses beyond 4 per cent of his income.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I realize that. I do not want to interrupt the parliamentary assistant but I have only a few minutes left. Peculiarly enough, in the case to which I have referred the child was 16 in January. Therefore the parent had his exemption cut from $400 to $150 because of one payment in December, received one payment in January and then got no more. I admit it is an odd case, but that is what happened. I maintain that in those circumstances he should not even have had to apply for family allowance. He did not want to apply and he should not have had to do so. Whether or not he received the cheque he would still have been in the same position.
The small income groups are in a very sad plight today because of the taxation in this country. They are gradually losing their savings. I know of many who have cashed insurance policies in order to keep going, to pay for illnesses and the many other things which beset a family. That is largely as the result of the heavy taxes levied upon them. Taxes for what? To reduce the national debt? They were not consulted whether or not they wanted to reduce the national debt, and the house was not consulted as to whether or not it wished to reduce the national debt. Yet these people are paying taxes for that purpose. In the last five years the national debt has been reduced by $2,344 million, an
The Budget-Mr. Weaver average of $33J per person per annum. For a family of five it is $167i per annum or $837J for the five years.
That would go a long way toward the ownership of a small house. With housing loans reduced and credit restrictions in force the little fellow has not much of a chance. The thing that builds a nation is the faith of its people and their pride. On Tuesday last the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said, as found at page 1513 of Hansard:
When a man owns his home he has his roots in the soil; he is a citizen; he belongs to the country and to a certain part of it.
I submit that if an agent or trustee were given money by an individual with which to purchase a house for him and when he requested possession of the house he was told, "Sorry, but you owed some money elsewhere and I applied your payments on your debt; you do not own a house", the law would take a very dim view of the agent's activities. In fact he would find himself in a very precarious legal position. If the minister believes the national debt should be reduced let him say so. Let him put into the budget an amount for that specific purpose and not call it public buildings which cannot be built, clothing for the forces which cannot be used, equipment which is not required, and then turn round and say to the little fellow: Sorry, we could not use your money for that so we paid your debts.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago this month I took part in another budget debate in this chamber, and congratulated the government on their handling of the affairs of this country. At that time I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to lend a sympathetic ear to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his plans for the development of the west under P.F.R.A. At the same time I asked him to lend a sympathetic ear to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in any plans he might bring forward respecting railway development in our great northland. I also asked the Minister of Finance to take as his yardstick in financing and government spending the words of an eastern farmer: "Break the back forty acres before you build a new front porch". I said I would ask the minister to move in that direction as far and as fast as our resources would permit.
Unfortunately war broke out in Korea shortly after that, which brought heavy demands upon the economy of Canada, and I could not expect very much headway to be made in the direction I had pointed out. However, as I look back I find that considerable progress has been made. I find that the
1560	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Weaver Lynn Lake railway to which I referred at that time is daily pushing further and further into that northland. Since that time P.F.R.A. surveys have been carried out in an area which I described in that address. Two years ago I spoke of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) looking northward; these were the words I used, at page 1839 of Hansard for 1950:
-looking northward at a treasure house beside which fabulous wealth, to which the genie of Aladdin's lamp had access, was peanuts.
i went on to illustrate, and spoke of the Flin Flon mine. This is what I said at that time, at page 1840 of Hansard:
The Flin Flon mine went into production in 1930 with ore reserves at that time of 19 million tons. Today Flin Flon is a town of 10,000 persons. In 1949 it produced $37 million worth of metals. It paid directly into the treasury of the people of Canada in income taxes and ore royalties, more than $5,500,000, and indirectly another $1,500,000. Considering the 10,000 people who derive their livelihood from that mine, they have contributed from five to seven and one-half times the national average towards the revenues of $2,500 million collected last year by the Minister of Finance.
I have before me the annual report of that same company for 1951, and I want to point out the further progress that has been made. The revenue from that mine in 1951 instead of $37 million was $54,250,000. Instead of paying $5,500,000 into the treasury of the people of Canada the figure was $12,100,000. Instead of $1,500,000 paid indirectly, the figure is now $3 million. The total revenue of the government last year was not doubled, however; instead of the $2,500 million I mentioned in 1950 it was $4,000 million, an increase of only 60 per cent. So the figure I mentioned of from five to seven and one-half times the national average, as representing the wealth created by these people, now has become from seven to ten times the national average. As I said at that time, it was surely something to gladden the heart of the Minister of Finance to find such revenues coming from these mines in northern Canada.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I am going to lift the lid of the treasure box and give you a further glimpse into what you may expect to come out of the northland in the near future. I will deal for a moment with the railway picture, starting with the very poorest. The Lynn Lake railway is opening up a new mining development which has turned the eyes of the people to northern Manitoba. With the movement of the town of Sherridon to Lynn Lake, that railway reaches far into the north. It is only about 100 miles from a place called Brochet on Reindeer lake, which itself is only a short jump from Uranium City in northern Saskatchewan, which in the not far distant


future will be a town of 5,000 people, and which requires railway facilities. Once you reach that point it is only another short jump to Pine Point on Great Slave lake, where is one of the greatest undeveloped ore bodies in the world. At that point you are down to an elevation of 600 feet, and can follow along the Mackenzie river to a point where it is just a short jump to Alaska. If you take a globe-there is no point in looking at an ordinary map-and draw a line from central Alaska through this area to eastern Canada you will find that the shortest route from Alaska to the industrial areas of the east is via Lynn Lake and on down through Manitoba.
Up in northern Manitoba we have the Hudson Bay railway, which has been mentioned many times in this house. I do not think many people realize just what that railway means at the present time. Last year 7,250,000 bushels of wheat were shipped over that route. That in itself puts the Hudson Bay railway in the black. There are certain savings because of the short route to Europe. Those savings do not necessarily come back to Canada, but somebody gets them, and they are just like sugar scattered out to attract ants, the ants in this case being the ships that can make money coming to Churchill to pick up wheat. The more ships that come, the more wheat will be shipped from there, so today that is a paying proposition for the people of Canada in spite of any minor deficits that may show in the balance sheets. I can assure this house that those deficits will be wiped out in the very near future. Interests in Zurich, Switzerland, are interested in taking out 200,000 tons of pulpwood a year through the port of Churchill. This year they are taking out a trial shipment of
5.000	cords. I will try to put this in figures which will be easy to understand. Those
200.000	tons of pulpwood will mean revenue to the Hudson Bay railway equal to that from 8 million bushels of wheat. So no one in the east and no one in this house need feel that if they do see a small deficit in the accounts, they are paying for the upkeep of something that is not of value to this country.
I would like to mention another point in regard to this northern area. Last year 22 million pounds of fish were shipped out of northern Manitoba. This year 30 million pounds of fish were shipped out of northern Manitoba, and there are going to be many large increases as the Lynn Lake railway keeps working north.
I turn now to the mining picture. Few people know that northern Manitoba is the coming nickel capital of the world. I think I am conservative in this estimate; some

people may dispute it but I am being careful to be conservative. Approximately 75 per cent of the ore reserves of nickel on this globe are in northern Manitoba. There are four potential Sudburys in northern Manitoba. To indicate further that I have some knowledge of that of which I speak, may I say that I know personally that in one of these potential Sudburys there are five tremendous ore bodies. One of those ore bodies is sheared diagonally from one side at the top to the bottom so that the ore body gets smaller as it goes down but the piece that is sheared off gets larger as it goes down. Above 1,000 feet of this one ore body the ore that has been blocked out equals one-quarter of a billion tons. There are 250 million tons of ore above 1,000 feet; and that is not all the ore above 1,000 feet in this one block out of five. In terms of the present value of nickel, that ore is worth $6.50 a ton.
Again, to give you a comparison of what that means in value, may I say that down in Utah where they have a large copper mining development they mine, by open pit method, ore that is worth $3 ai ton. It is a large type of operation. I have not looked up the figures in recent years but they started to develop, in 1940, an operation that would mine 25,000 tons a day of that copper ore; and before they had completed the plant they doubled the size of it to 50,000 tons a day. That is the type of operation that we shall see in northern Manitoba in the not far distant future.
Lest some people misunderstand what I am saying, I would point out that this has no connection with Lynn Lake. Lynn Lake is a relatively small, high-grade nickel operation that completely justifies the railway that isi going in there now. But these other properties are away beyond that. Lynn Lake cannot be compared with them. In fact, this one little piece I have outlined to you has eight times the ore reserves blocked out at Lynn Lake up to the end of 1949. There are huge nickel ore bodies there. These nickel ore bodies compare in size with the iron ore of Labrador. As you know, nickel is worth something between 60 cents and 70 cents a pound, as compared with the relatively low price of iron. That will give you some conception of the development that is now under way in Manitoba.
The first time that I heard of this nickel ore body was when flying with a prospector only three years ago. Drilling had been just started on this block at that time. He did not know the values and I had no idea at that time what the values of this ore would be. But he described to me the ore body, because it came right to the surface. He did not know
The Budget-Mr. Weaver what it was but he described the size of it to me. I estimated at that time that that ore body would be of the order of 400 million tons. From then on I was curious as to what the content of it would be. When I found the content of it I placed it on the records of this house. The future is terrific for that part of the country.
I might say that this reef, as you would call it, runs for approximately 300 miles. To give you a little bit of an idea of what happened, may I say this. In the days when the world was young by some upheaval the crust was broken, and these fluid, metal-bearing ores were squeezed up as the crust shifted and came back. That is how our mines of certain types were laid down many years ago.
Copper is one of the metals in short supply in the world today. The copper picture is exceedingly favourable in northern Manitoba. Not far from this new reef that runs so far, there is a similar reef that is copper bearing. It would not surprise me if the same thing that applies to nickel is later found to apply to copper.
I know of another mine; it is a tungsten mine. Tungsten is something that is in exceedingly short supply at the present time. This mine has rich ore, and it will be brought into production in the not far distant future. There are many small mines that cannot go into production because they have no power. It is only the big operations that can bring power to them. The power picture in northern Manitoba is something out of this world. To give you an idea of it, let me say this. You have all heard of the Saskatchewan river and the power development along the Saskatchewan river. You have heard of the power development along the Red river and the Winnipeg river. The Red river watershed which runs down into the United States pours all its waters into lake Winnipeg. The Saskatchewan river, from both north and south watersheds, pours its waters into lake Winnipeg. Out of the north end of lake Winnipeg runs the Nelson river to Hudson bay, a drop of about 850 feet. Along that river, from source to mouth, is approximately 2J million horsepower that can be generated by water power; it is there to be developed but is still undeveloped.
One of the large developments is at White Mud falls. It is the first. It lies not far from the north end of lake Winnipeg. I have been told by responsible authorities that survey parties were out there last year and that they will be out there in larger numbers this year, and thaF the power from that development will be required in southern Manitoba inside of seven years. When I say it will

The Budget-Mr. Weaver be required, I do not mean that the development will have to start then; the development will have to be completed and will have to be turning out power inside of seven years. The moment it starts turning out power, numerous mines will open up in this area. You can talk about the resources in northern Alberta, and in northern Ontario and in northern Quebec. Canada is aware of those resources but is not aware of the fact that in northern Manitoba, having regard to its size and to its population, there are greater resources there than in any other place in Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or in the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; possibly in the world. Certainly those resources in older parts of the world have sustained populations of 50 million and 100 million people, not just
50,000	or 48,000 as there are in my constituency at the present time.
This area is in the Pre-Cambrian formation. These people require food. To give you an example of what that means, may I point out that in Flin Flon, Manitoba, we have to import our milk, and over half our milk comes from away out in Saskatchewan, from a place called Melfort, and it takes twenty-four hours by railroad to reach us. When you start bringing milk to 10,000 people, and you have to ship it on the train for twenty-four hours, you will see the problem in front of you, when you get larger populations in that area, to supply them with milk. I am going to make a forecast. I have made many forecasts in the past, and my batting average is fairly high. We have been talking about redistribution and the movement of population and the losing of population. Some people have worried about Manitoba losing a couple of seats this year. I am going to make this forecast. By the time of the next redistribution, that is within ten years, there will be 100,000 people in that area that I describe. According to the present quota of Canada that will be two constituencies. You never need to worry about Manitoba, as long as Canada exists, in respect of losing seats, because that province will more than keep up with the growth of Canada. But I am talking about this large population. They need food. They do not want to bring it long distances by rail, particularly milk.
Two years ago I described an area that has lain there dormant for many many years, which is known as the Saskatchewan river delta. All this water coming down from the western prairies over the years has dropped this silt from the prairies into this area until it is now 40 feet deep in places. It is marvellous agricultural land. To give you an

idea of the size of this area, it has been estimated by competent engineers that the area consists of 4 million acres. Hon. members know that Manitoba is a wheat-growing province, but only 2 million acres of wheat were grown in Manitoba last year. That will give hon. members some conception of the size of this area to which I refer.
When you go to bring in a new process in industry and you are not certain as to how it will work out, you first test it in the laboratory and then you take it to the pilot plant stage. We have the pilot plant stage in this huge development at The Pas, Manitoba. There is an area there known as the Pasquia river area. It is a small triangle that lies between the Pasquia and the Carrot rivers and the Manitoba and Saskatchewan boundaries, with the apex of this triangle at The Pas, Manitoba. To show you how much attention has been given to this area by engineers, but not by the public, I would point out that between 1914 and 1916 an expedition known as the Dunn inquiry examined this area and considered draining a very large lake there known as Cedar lake. During the period from 1921 to 1924 this was followed by an investigation under Mr. Horsey, an official of the then department of the interior. In 1946 a detailed survey of agriculture in this district was undertaken by Mr. F. W. Broderick, horticulturist, and Mr. S. E. Churniak, economist. I have before me all these reports. They are quite voluminous, and they are my authority for saying that people who are competent to study these things have gone into them. I have before me a soil survey report on the Carrot river reclamation project by Professor Ellis, of the university -of Manitoba. Mr. E. B. Paterson in 1947 prepared the engineering survey which I hold in my hand. We have a progress report on this Pasquia river development area, dated November 1, 1951-that is the triangle I am speaking of- which is worthy of consideration by anyone who is interested. I am going to tell you briefly what it contains, to give you an idea how much of that 4 million acres may be arable land. There are 135,000 acres that have been all surveyed. I am giving you the facts. Of those 135,000 acres, 96,000 acres are arable land, and a further 10,000 acres suitable for growing hay and grazing.
The cost to protect this area from floods, which is the great danger, because the Saskatchewan river overflows its banks from Cumberland House to The Pas periodically, and that is what built this delta, is estimated by the engineers at $1,350,000. Now, estimates are always turning out low, but assume it will cost $1,500,000 to protect these 100,000 acres, roughly, of arable land. That would work out at a cost of $15 an acre. There is

no place in the Dominion of Canada, there is no place anywhere, that you can get land as cheap as $15 an acre, and this is the very best land. It was put there in the first place by the Almighty to provide food for this great area, or the people in it, when the time arrived to develop it, which is now.
Objections have been raised regarding the climate. From my personal observation I can say that we do not need to worry about the climate. About three hundred years ago, when the first settlers came into Quebec, they had a very difficult time to survive because of the climate. If you read the early history of the St. Lawrence valley and the privations of the early settlers, you will realize that at that time the climate of the valley was considered a hard one. Our climate there is no worse than that. We have longer hours of sunshine in the summertime; we have a little longer winters, but so far as severity goes, I have been colder in Ottawa than I have ever been up there.
I am very interested in gardening. For many years I have raised a garden a hundred miles north of this area, and I picked ripe tomatoes in my garden on August 10. I have ripened egg plant in my garden. As a matter of fact there is nothing I cannot grow in my garden except corn, and grow it very successfully. However, I am not asking you to take my word for it. I asked an official of The Pas, Mr. F. B. Chalmers, superintendent of northern resources, who should know, to write me a letter on this, and I want to read some parts of it. He says:
Further to our discussion of this area with reference to frost damage, I have had a good many years of experience as a lands inspector for the Manitoba farms loans and am intimately familiar with many areas in Manitoba, as well as the Carrot river. It cannot, of course, be said that there is no danger from frost in the Carrot river; however, I feel confident that it may be definitely stated that there are several other sections of the province which are farmed successfully and are equally, if not more subject to frost than this particular area. This is rather an indefinite statement, but I feel justified in making it from the experience I have had.
I have spoken with several farmers who have farmed in this area over periods of from fifteen to twenty years and they tell me, of course, that at times they have had some frost, but that they have never experienced a total loss through frost.
I am interested in the subject of frost. I am going to tell you that frost can be a serious obstacle. This is an area that should be a mixed farming area. It is an area that should supply milk, grazing, hay, and coarse grains. This is something that the farmers will recognize, that you will make more money out of frosted grain feeding it to stock than you ever will make out of bread grain, raising it and selling it through the elevators. That, gentlemen, is the picture of that area. The principles of the Prairie Farm
The Budget-Mr. Weaver Rehabilitation Act should be extended from one end of Canada to the other to take care of propositions such as this because they are large propositions.
In 1947 it was estimated that it would cost $20 million to bring those 4 million acres into production. Let us assume that that was a low estimate, and that it would cost $40 million; that is still only $10 an acre for a tremendous area, which will support a population-or supports a similar population in other parts of Canada-of upwards of 60,000 persons, without the attendant services which go with those persons, That is something that is a little difficult for the financial structure of provincial governments.
Large sums of money have been spent in many provinces, based upon these principles, and they should be extended. I understand there is a bill that might have been introduced a number of times in the last few years, but that because of a lack of interest that bill has not come forward. It would extend these principles to other parts of Canada. I feel the cabinet should reconsider its position, and that the bill should be introduced and passed at this session.
This project will go ahead. If it failed to go ahead here, then any bright individual could go down to New York and get United States funds, without any question, sufficient to develop the area, But that is not what we want. We want these things developed as they have been developed in recent years.
We have heard criticisms in the house from the city of Winnipeg, because they feel they have lost their preferred position in connection with freight rates. Winnipeg has had a preferred position for many years in respect of freight rates, because of its location not far from the head of the lakes. But we must keep in mind that Canada is not made up of any one city or any one area. If Winnipeg has had something that should naturally fall to Edmonton, then it is time it did fall to Edmonton.
I will say this to the city of Winnipeg, that I do not think many people in that city are aware of what is taking place in the province of Manitoba. If they will forget the preferred position they had with respect to the area west of them on the prairies, and will look north, they will find an empire at their doorstep which will keep their resources going just as long as any of the people of that city would want.
One further quotation regarding this area I should like to give, and then I shall close my remarks. I read this once before, but repetition will do no harm and I shall read it again. This is from the address of Mr. S. W.

The Budget-Mr. G. S. White Fairweather, vice-president of research and development for the Canadian National Railways, of Montreal, before the Engineering Institute of Canada and the Association of Professional Engineers of the province of Manitoba in Winnipeg, on Thursday, January 12, 1950. He said:
The subject which I intend to discuss is of particular interest to those who are developing what I have elsewhere termed the "frontier fringe of Canada." In many countries the word "frontier" has a grim significance but the frontier of which I speak is not a dividing line between nations, it is a dividing line between the developed and the undeveloped. Beyond it lies opportunity, a challenge to the venturesome and a sure hope of reward to industry, intelligence and perseverance. By the definition of my term, the frontier of which I speak is not static. It is being pushed back year by year. It has receded far beyond the position it occupied along the coast and the St. Lawrence river 200 years ago. Only one life-span ago this city of Winnipeg with all its present amenities of civilization was on the frontier fringe. Development pressed westward from the east and eastward from the west until from ocean to ocean the natural resources of Canada were made available in a belt of varying width. Now the path of development lies northward and much of what we regarded not many decades ago as a hostile, barren waste is proving to be a storehouse of wealth-the reward of the hardy, modern pioneer. The rock drill and the mine shaft may have replaced the plow and the grain elevator as symbols of development; but whether the development is of the forest, the fisheries, agriculture or mining, the end objective must be profit to the individual and an increase in national wealth.
Hon. members, we are building a nation today, a nation such as has never been known before on the face of the globe, a nation such as this globe will never see again.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like most sincerely to congratulate the hon. member who has just completed his remarks upon having made a most interesting and instructive address, and having given us a glimpse into the future, and of the great natural resources existing in his province. Through his kindness I was one of the privileged few who, when the party visited Churchill, were taken to his home town of Flin Flon, and were there able to see something of the great development at the Hudson bay mine.
I liked in particular one remark of the hon, member when he referred to the national outlook. It seems to me that many times Canadians are too provincial in their outlook, and we overlook the fact that anything that benefits one part of Canada benefits all Canadians, in the long run.
In taking part in this debate I wish to direct my remarks to the national emergency existing today in Canada in regard to dairy products, and in particular to the tragic


plight of the cheese producers. No one can deny the seriousness of the situation facing these producers today.
Three cold facts have to be faced: First, there is the effect of substantial imports of dairy products from other countries; secondly, the loss of the United Kingdom and United States markets for dairy products; and, thirdly the problem of the huge surplus of milk in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, due to the United States embargo on importations of dairy cattle from Canada brought about by the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. There is no getting away from these three facts. They have created an emergency so far as the cheese producers are concerned.
It is a well recognized and widely accepted fact that the dairy industry plays an important part in the health of any nation and that, consequently, its importance to the Canadian economy must be weighed in a balance that takes this factor into account, even though the value of such a factor is difficult to set forth in plain dollars and cents.
Leaving that aside, let us consider the known factors. First, there are 450,000 farm families, representing over three millions of people in Canada, who are directly dependent upon the dairy industry for the major part of their livelihood. Secondly, there are thousands of people engaged in dairy manufacture and distribution who, in addition, are indirectly dependent upon the dairy industry for their living. Then, thirdly, there are plants and equipment in Canada represented by over
11,000	creameries, over 500 Cheddar cheese factories, and some 150 combined butter and cheese factories, hundreds of fluid milk distributing plants, as well as many factories engaged in evaporating and condensing milk, and in the production of powdered milk, ice cream, processed cheese, and the like. All these are operated wholly by the dairy industry.
The dairy industry contributes well over half a billion dollars per annum to the farmers of Canada. The value of dairy products at the factories and milk plants is approximately $454 million, while the value of dairy products used on the farm is well over $105 million. Today some wonder if the industry is sufficiently important to worry about. I think it is, for many reasons.
Over the years it has been proved that the dairy industry is the most stable branch of agriculture, being less prone to weather and other economic ills which appear from time to time. Dairy products have assumed an indispensable place in the diet of this country which we associate with a high standard of living. The dairy industry is the cornerstone

of our economic stability. It is essential for the maintenance of soil fertility. There are millions of people in the world today who require and need better food, without which there is less likelihood of a peaceful understanding of each other.
In so far as this country is concerned it is imperative that dairying be made sufficiently attractive to ensure its remaining one of our major industries. During the war years we were never faced with any question of overproduction or surplus of dairy products. In fact during those years the government encouraged the farmer to increase his production in every way. The farmer was encouraged to increase his stock and to put new acreage under production. Thus the farmer was able to greatly increase the production of food.
During those years farm labour was scarce because no one wanted to work on the farm. Labour wanted to work in industry in the cities at higher wages. The dairy producer, despite the shortage of labour and the scarcity and expense of farm machinery and all the other difficulties that faced him, was able to play his part. He increased his stock and he cultivated more acres. Thus there was additional food available, not only for ourselves but for our allies.
During those years the farmer did not have a price tag on his products because the government strictly controlled the price of farm products. As far as cheese was concerned, during those years it was all requisitioned by the government. This did not apply to industry. Not only during war years but later on, until today industry has operated on a cost-plus basis. Every article manufactured by industry sells at a figure that will return to the manufacturer, not only his cost of production but a fair profit in addition. It is quite clear now that wartime controls and the policies of the government in force since the war cost the dairy producer hundreds of millions of dollars.
It seems to me that the government should take some action to reimburse the dairy producers of Ontario and Quebec for the losses they have sustained. Apparently the government recognized that it had some responsibility in the matter, although I will not say it was a legal responsibility, because only a short time ago it approved the payment of $65 million to reimburse the western farmers who during the war years and since had sold their farm products under practically the same conditions as the farm products of Ontario and Quebec were sold. That action indicated the advantage to any group of producers in Canada of being well organized,
The Budget-Mr. G. S. White in being able to exert pressure on the government and in having members in the house making insistent demands on their behalf.
As everyone knows, farmers do not work on a 40, 44 or 48 hour week as does industry. If they did, the cost of dairy products would be much higher than it is today. The farmer continually hears over the radio or reads in the press of new wage demands, of demands for better working conditions for labour. Every time there is an increase in wages to labour the price of the manufactured article which the farmer has to pay increases while the prices he receives for his dairy products remain the same or in many cases decrease. The dairy producer is simply asking that in this emergency, and it must be classed as an emergency, the government take immediate and proper steps to save this vital industry.
I have mentioned the part played by the dairy farmer during the war. If war comes again he will be expected to produce more food under practically the same conditions which existed from 1940 to 1946. It is the opinion of many thinking Canadian citizens that it is in the interests of Canada to maintain and support a dairy industry as a defence measure.
There is a further obligation on the government to the hundreds of veterans who used their gratuities and re-establishment credits to set themselves up in farming. These veterans have heavy commitments to meet over the years stretching into the future. If they are to be successful in re-establishing themselves in the peacetime economy of our country, then the veteran farmers must receive a fair price for their dairy products.
Farming, including dairy farming, has become a much more expensive business than it was years ago. The capital outlay and operating expenses are much higher. The type of labour required calls for more skill, and all in all the business demands that it be operated at full capacity. When you have a high producing cost the need for efficiency is greater than ever before. The dairy farmer today is finding that year by year the cost of farm labour is increasing and that other expenses such as municipal taxes, hydro, telephone, repairs, freight rates and the articles used by him in the operation of his farm have increased over what they were in 1951.
In addition, the cost of operating the cheese factory has increased to the same degree. The wages of a man who draws the milk, the wages of the cheese maker and the wages of other help are all up over 1951, as are the costs of fuel, supplies, repairs and
