The Budget-Mr. G. S. White everything else. The speech from the throne delivered in February, 1950, contained this paragraph:
Circumstances outside Canada have been responsible for some downward adjustment in the price of farm products. Measures have already been taken to reduce the impact of these adjustments. In order to provide authority for continuing price support to that end for the primary products of our farms and fisheries, you will be asked to amend the Agricultural Products Act, the Agricultural Prices Support Act and the Fisheries Prices Support Act.
Apparently in February 1950 the government felt that it had some responsibility for continuing price support for the primary products of the farm. If the government felt that price support was necessary for dairy products in February, 1950, surely the need is much greater today with the loss of the United Kingdom and United States markets and United States embargo on Canadian cattle. The words "outside of Canada" used in 1950 did not relieve the government of all its responsibility because some of the circumstances which have put the dairy industry on the rocks today happened inside this country.
The outlook is grim indeed for the dairy producers of Canada if the government does not recognize that and has no plan for correcting its errors. The importing of millions of pounds of cheese from other countries did not benefit the Canadian cheese producer. The importation of vegetable oils and the use of substitutes for cream and milk did not help the dairy producer. Today we find many bakeries, which formerly used thick cream and milk, now using a filled product, the chief ingredient of which is imported into Canada. The uses to which this filling can be put are practically endless.
Nor can the government escape some measure of responsibility for the manner in which the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease was handled by the officials of the Department of Agriculture. The dairy producer has to compete with imported vegetable oils and fats, and fats extracted from imported seeds and grains. Where these fats are of domestic origin the dairy farmer has to meet that competition. However, in the case of fats derived from imports it seems to me that the dairy producer has a perfect right to demand from the federal authorities, who have control of tariffs and excise taxes, the same protection readily afforded other industries which affect far fewer people than the hundreds of thousands of Canadians engaged in agriculture.
It is admitted, and it is true, that by reason of our climatic conditions the Canadian dairy producer cannot at all seasons produce


dairy products as cheaply as countries more favourably situated or where competitive wages and standards of living are lower. I am sure no one will argue that producers of dairy products in Canada should accept lower returns to meet competition from these countries. As long as the Canadian farmer is doing his job efficiently, he is entitled to equality in hours of labour and living conditions with the rest of the Canadian people.
The two main items of costs, wages and prices of concentrated feeds, are beyond the control of the average dairy farmer, and as long as they remain at the present prices we will never have cheap milk. The only factors the farmer can control are the volume and quality of his crops and the care he gives his herd. It is interesting to note that at the recent cheese board held at the city of Belleville no cheese was purchased. As the result of that all other boards have been cancelled. I noticed yesterday in the Ottawa Journal a report of a meeting at Vankleek Hill on April 22 of eastern Ontario cheese men who asked for a 33 cent floor price for cheese. I should like to quote two paragraphs from the remarks made by the chairman of the meeting, Mr. John A. Fraser. He said:
In order to survive in eastern Ontario producers of milk for cheese factories had to get from $2.75 to $3 per hundredweight for 3-5 milk. If cheese reverted to the last year's floor of 28 to 29 cents factories would be padlocked in eastern Ontario. From 20 to 30 small factories definitely would have to close their doors.
In the same paper there is an editorial on the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture in the house with respect to the questions asked by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) and myself. The editorial is headed, "Mr. Gardiner Backs Away From the Cheese Crisis". After reviewing the situation, the editorial sums up the present situation as follows:
The net result is the threat of a chaotic tangle in the entire Ontario dairy industry, possibly in Quebec as well. Cheese exchanges, where the trade buys from the factories, are closed and the trade is not buying. Many factories have not opened. Cows will soon all be on pasture and a huge flow of milk threatens to back up right to the top grade. This could well threaten the livelihood of several hundred thousand persons in Ontario alone, could result in widespread unemployment. It is certainly
The Budget-Mr. G. S. White a situation which requires something better than the evasive answer Mr. Gardiner gave in the house last week.
I should also like to refer to the chamber of commerce resolutions for 1951-52 in their chapter on agriculture. They make this statement:
It believes that acreage controls, delivery quotas and governmental marketing monopolies should be limited to times of extreme national emergency . . .
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that the present condition in the dairy industry is a national emergency brought about by conditions over which the dairy producer had no control. As the editorial points out, this emergency condition affects hundreds of thousands of Canadians and may be the cause of widespread unemployment, for if the dairy producer cannot sell his product certainly he cannot buy the product of industry. Almost any implement dealer in eastern Ontario can tell of the many contracts he had on file for the delivery of tractors and other implements this spring which have been cancelled.
Any attempt by the minister to evade the issue or to place the responsibility upon any provincial government will not be accepted by the dairy producer, and will not meet this emergency which cannot be handled either by the producers or within any province. The loss of our two markets, the United Kingdom market and the United States market because of the embargo following the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, created a condition the cheese producers could not handle. I am sure the minister is aware of the many meetings that have been held in eastern Ontario during the past six weeks. I am sure he must have received many petitions and resolutions asking that a floor price be established for cheese. As I mentioned a moment ago, the meeting at Vankleek Hill asked for a floor price of 33 cents. The meeting in Belleville on April 19 asked for a floor price of 36 cents.
I appeal to the minister to recognize the emergency that exists today in the dairy industry, an industry which affects the whole economy of Canada so greatly. I cannot believe he meant by his remarks last Monday that no floor price will be set for cheese. Surely he will agree that this large number of Canadians are entitled to assistance during this emergency period by means of a floor price that will at the very least permit the dairy farmer to produce his product with a small margin of profit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am
one of those Canadians, Mr. Speaker, who paid their income taxes in the last few weeks.
I do not suppose that makes me an expert on this budget. However I can tell you it permits me to speak with greater feeling than might otherwise have been possible. I believe that taxes in Canada are too high, and I think some way must toe found to bring about reductions.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduced his budget shortly before Easter, he certainly presented Canadians with a sobering document. In a nutshell, he is proposing to take from the pockets of the people this year a sum of $4-5 billion or better. What is the significance of that figure to the average taxpayer? In the first place, it means that this year the federal government is going to take 21 cents in taxes, out of every dollar which is earned in the country. In the second place, it means that the federal government in 1952 is going to take from every man, woman and child in this nation average taxes of $320. This compares with a per capita tax in 1939 of only $40. Strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, when I was home at Easter I did not find too many of my constituents worried about that fact. I think the main reason for the apparent public apathy is the number of anaesthetic devices that the government has developed in recent years, to ease the pain in extracting the taxpayers' dollar. About 99 out of every 100 taxpayers in Canada pay the 10 per cent sales tax, the 15 per cent luxury tax, cigarette taxes, excise taxes, customs duties, tariffs, in blissful ignorance of the amount which is going to the federal treasury. As a matter of fact, even where personal income taxes are concerned much of it is collected by the employer. Even if you go to the employee and ask him how much he is paying the federal government in personal income taxes he has not the vaguest idea.
For that reason, I think Canadians have not as yet realized the significance of the astronomical figures which the Minister of Finance presented here a few weeks ago, nor have they realized the seriousness of those figures. I think it is a tragedy that, for one year at least, we cannot have Canadians pay all their federal taxes in one lump sum. If they had to do that, there would not be a revolution, but I venture to say the government would not last one week unless they brought taxes down. I say that the level of taxation in Canada has reached the danger point. I believe it has reached a level where


it is lowering our standard of living. It has reached a point where it is discouraging initiative on the farm, in the factory, and throughout business generally. It has reached a level where it is harming trade, and is promoting inflation.
More than a year ago the Minister of Finance made a proposition to this house with which I wholeheartedly agreed. He said this, in effect. There is no magic in government finance. A dollar which is given to one person must, first of all, be taken away from another. $4-5 billion is a lot of money. I think no one should feel that this money can be raised simply by "soaking the rich". Let no citizen make any mistake. These expenditures are going to be paid for by the average Canadian, the workingman, the farmer and the small businesfsman. I realize that our national production is high, but I do not think it has reached a point where we can take $4-5 billion in federal taxes without having serious repercussions. I shall, therefore, propose this evening, that our federal expenditures should be cut by at least $315 million. It is fair for the minister to ask me "how" and "where". I shall try to tell him.
The government would have us believe that this budget is the price which we have to pay for security. But is it? I remind hon. members that the greater part of this budget is for items that have no relation whatever to defence. In his budget speech last year, the Minister of Finance stated that the necessities of defence now require that our expenditures for all other purposes should be reduced. Yet despite that statement the minister has come before parliament with a proposal that non-defence expenditures be increased by at least $227 million. Personally, I cannot agree that, in view of our defence emergency, non-defence expenditures should continue to grow and grow. Many of the items in this budget are desirable, in fact most of them are desirable, and most of them are for items that Canadians would like. But I think if it means getting the tax level down, Canadians would just as soon do without some of them.
Since coming to Ottawa I have been one of those who have always believed there was a good deal of merit in the suggestion that a commission be set up somewhat along the lines of the Hoover commission in the United States, to study waste and duplication in the government. I think a good deal could be accomplished by such a commission, because *certainly members of parliament have not the time nor the facilities to go through the estimates and the public accounts, and give

them the scrutiny that they deserve. This evening I desire to make a number of concrete proposals of instances where I think the minister could save money. I realize that some of the suggestions may not be popular; nevertheless, I think they are sensible. I shall classify these savings in three categories: First, petty savings; second, major savings which are dependent more or less upon government policy; third, savings in the defence effort.
In the first category, I maintain that the estimates are cluttered up with dozens of petty expenditures which no sound business concern would maintain in a time of financial emergency. I should like to give a few examples. I refer the house to the estimates, first to items 54 and 55. In these items the government proposes to spend $2,039,000 for international shortwave broadcast services. If I understand these services correctly, they beam broadcasts to countries in Europe, and particularly behind the iron curtain. In the first place, I doubt if there are many people in those countries who have radios powerful enough to receive the broadcasts. But even admitting that the broadcasts have a certain propaganda value, even admitting that they may create certain good' will for Canadians, I believe that their value is far outweighed by the cost.
I suggest to this house tonight that this item might be classified as a luxury expenditure under present circumstances. I believe it should be deleted from the estimates1, in order to save the taxpayer $2,000,000.
The second saving I would suggest has to do with the House of Commons itself. After all, if hon. members are really interested in making savings I think they should set an example. For three straight years, ever since the inception of the 21st parliament, we have had double sessions. As nearly as I can gather, the last double session of parliament cost the taxpayers of Canada directly $2 million, and indirectly I suppose a good deal more money. Surely, if our rules were modernized, if they were brought up to date, it should be possible for this parliament to get through its work in four or five months at most. There are other disadvantages to these double sessions. After all, it is difficult for a member to get around to see his constituents if he has to be down here eight or nine months of the year. I think too if they are persisted in, they will discourage many members from offering themselves for parliament, because of the time involved1 at Ottawa. There is a good deal of talk of another fall session this year. I sincerely hope that this may not be necessary. Let us sit and get
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher our work done by July. I do not think it is fair to ask the taxpayers to pay the cost of another double session.
The third saving which I would suggest is of a minor nature; it has been made in this parliament before. For the first time, this year, it is proposed to pay lieutenant governors a special allowance, "hospitality" and "entertainment." Personally, I have always felt that the work done by these gentlemen could be just as effectively performed by our chief justices. However, whether or not that is so, I do not think that at a time when the taxpayers are facing expenditures of $4-5 billion, they should be called upon to pay bills for entertainment and hospitality for these gentlemen. If item 170 were deleted from the estimates, the amount of $86,000 could be saved.
The fourth saving I would suggest has to do with the printing of departmental reports and other publications. This year the government is going to spend $7 million on this item; and in addition it proposes to spend $10,500,000 on films, displays, advertising and so forth. Of course, some of these pamphlets are valuable; I do not deny that. But there are a great number-and I think the number is growing-which have very dubious value. I have several in my hand which came to my office this week. Two of them are from the Department of National Health and Welfare. One of them contains a series of cartoons. One of the cartoons shows a workingman having his hand held by a nurse. It says: "The nurse and the pulse of industry." For the life of me I cannot see of what value such pamphlets are to the taxpayers of Canada. I will venture to say that there is not one member in this house who does not consign regularly each week forty or fifty of these pamphlets to the wastepaper basket. I wish that the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary assistant would order the queen's printer to assemble all these publications and pamphlets in the railway committee room, and then I wish he would invite members of parliament to see the exhibition. I will wager that not only would the members get an eye-opener, but so also would the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his question and I should like to answer it. I wonder whether it is sensible to pay old age
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher pensions or family allowances to those with an income say of $5,000 a year or more. I take that figure out of the air, as perhaps it should be $6,000. I am referring to those people who have no need of them. If the minister adopted this suggestion my closest estimate is that he would save the taxpayers about $30 million.
Today there are about twenty different branches or agencies buying supplies or materials for the federal government. They are buying food, coal, paint, munitions, office equipment and things of that kind. It seems to me that so many purchasing departments cannot help but promote inefficiency ' and duplication. I remember Mr. Bryce, one of the officials of the Department of Finance, appearing last year before the public accounts committee. He told us that the Department of National Defence bought its cars direct from the manufacturers while the other departments did not, and as a result paid considerably higher price. Such a policy cost the taxpayer a good deal of money. I doubt if there is a single corporation in Canada with more than one purchasing department. Some years ago the province of Saskatchewan set up a central purchasing department and they have been most gratified with the results obtained. Such a central purchasing department for the federal government would mean a saving of about $10 million in the extra discounts that could be obtained through volume buying.
The savings in this category which I have mentioned would amount to roughly $81 million. If we add those to the first category, the savings would total about $91 million in non-defence expenditures.
Finally I come to the touchy defence figures. I would be the first to admit that I am not an expert on international affairs or national defence, but I do not think that that means that I as a federal representative should regard these expenditures as sacrosanct or beyond the pale of criticism.
It is proposed in the coming fiscal year to spend between $2,000 million and $2,500 million on rearmament and defence generally. It is incredible that a peace-loving nation like Canada only a few years after world war II should face commitments of this size.
I think everyone realizes that we are living in dangerous times and it is sensible and necessary to have adequate defences. However after having been home for a few weeks I can say to the minister that there are many Canadians who are viewing with great uneasiness the size of our rearmament program. They realize that every dollar spent on arms means $1 less spent on constructive national development.
1574	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
Is this money being spent wisely by national defence? I think every hon. member realizes that parliament, or even the efficient treasury board, has very little direct control over the detailed expenditures which are made for national defence. Today the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is spending more than $2,000 million,-more money than the whole government was spending shortly before Korea, and almost as much as is being spent this year by all his colleagues together. He is spending four times what the whole government was spending in 1939. While the minister may be the ablest minister in the world I do not think it is physically possible for him, or any one person, to go over these detailed defence expenditures, and say that they are being handled without waste or inefficiency.
The fact is that the military authorities have the responsibility for most of these military expenditures. I am not sure that the Canadian taxpayer is convinced that these gentlemen are not spending his money with too much abandon. I do not think the Canadian taxpayer is a bit impressed with the efforts at economy which the government has made in this connection. I feel the Department of National Defence is the department where the greatest economies in the budget can be made. I remember when Mr. Bryce, Mr. Drury and certain other officials appeared before the public accounts committee a year or so ago. Why, for instance, are we operating today in some cities a recruiting office for each of the three services?
I remember the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) pointing out to the public accounts committee that in that city there was a recruiting office for the navy, one for the air force and one for the army, all within a few blocks of each other. There are other savings of that kind which could be made. I remind the house that a few months ago Winston Churchill pared the defence budget of Great Britain substantially. I also remind the house that a week or so ago the United States congress was impressed with the need for economy. I have a press dispatch carrying the story. The heading of the article is, "Slash Advised in U.S. Budget". The article reads in part:
A $4,240,638,500 cut in the United States defence department's $50,921,022,770 budget for the fiscal year starting July 1 was recommended today by the House of Representatives appropriations committee.
If Great Britain and the United States can set such an example I do not see why it would not be sensible for Canada to follow the same course. If we could cut our budget


by 10 per cent, leaving it to the military to decide where they want it cut, we could save the taxpayers of Canada $225 million. I remind the house once again of the words of the Minister of Finance last year. He said that there was no magic in government financing, and that a dollar paid out to one person must first of all be taken from another. High taxes are not inevitable but if they are not inevitable, then expenses must be cut.
I think I have suggested savings approximating $315 million, and if there is something wrong with my suggestions let the minister point it out. I say that peacetime taxes in Canada have become too high. The government is taking 21 cents out of every dollar earned, on top of provincial and municipal taxation and have reached a point where most Canadians can no longer stand them. My main criticism of the budget must be that the federal government has not persevered in its efforts to curtail federal expenditures.

In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal largely with finance, and I want to refer to an article appearing in a pamphlet of the Canadian Construction Association. Any lack of confidence in the future appears to result from a fear of a recurrence of the thirties. Well, if the hon. member gets any comfort from that he is welcome to it. Yesterday he accused the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) and the minister of trying to trick the people in connection with his resolution regarding the four per cent floor under medical expenses. I was in the house at the time that resolution was adopted, and just when the discussion finished the hon. member hollered "unanimously". Well, there is no question about it; the house adopted the resolution unanimously. But the resolution only requested the government to consider the suggestion. The house did not unanimously adopt the resolution in the form the hon. member tried to twist it in order to bring the minister and the government to their knees. The government will consider it, and if in course of time they think it feasible, it will be brought in. But let us make no mistake about it; we voted that the government should consider the matter and nothing more.
Yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) had a good deal to say. At times he worked himself almost into a fury, attacking the government, attacking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), attacking the parliamentary assistant, and in general attacking the budget. He went on to say that the per capita taxation this year amounted to $300. The hon. member for Moose Jaw upped that tonight and made it $320. Then the hon. member for Eglinton said that the average family of five paid $1,750. If you multiply 300 by 5 it makes 1,500, not 1,750, so the hon. member was wrong there. Now let us see the per capita position as far as income is concerned. In 1951 the national income was $17 billion, 230 million; the population was 14 million, and the per capita income was $1,231, or $6,155 for a family of five. Let us . turn to 'he Tory regime and listen to them howl.


In 1935 the national income was $3 billion, 188 million; the population was 10,800,000 and the per capita income was $295 or $1,475 for a family of five. However, most people look at what they have left for themselves after paying taxes. The average income per family of five in 1951 was $6,155; taxes were $1,500, leaving that family $4,655. Under the Tory regime in 1935 a family of five with an income of $1,475 and taxes of $155 had only $1,320 for themselves. In 1951, after sixteen years of Liberal government the family of five-the Eglinton family, as I call it-have for themselves an income of $4,655, so in spite of what the hon. member says they are better off now than ever before. I would not call this a Hallowe'en budget, as the hon. member called it. Nor would I call it a budget with a false face. I would call it a sunshine budget. I would say the people of Canada have seen the light, that they have seen what a good government can do in reducing the national debt so there will be more sunshine for future Canadians.
Now we will leave the hon. member for Eglinton and talk about the financial critic of the opposition. I sent a note over to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) a while ago saying I was going to mention those two members. I am sorry they are not here tonight, but that is their responsibility. At page 1473 of Hansard the financial critic quoted Mr. Muir, president of the Royal Bank, as questioning whether the government was justified in raising such huge revenues. As you know, bankers make it their business to lend money. When they see prosperity in Canada getting to the point where people do not have to borrow so much, or can borrow from the government, so the banks make less and less money, naturally any banker in the country will not think that is good business. I would suggest that at this time there be less borrowing by governments, and that we carry our public works program and our social service program through the Bank of Canada, instead of borrowing from the private banks.
Then at page 1478 the financial critic accused the government of debasing or debauching the currency of Canada. Unlike Nelson, who had at least one good eye, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) held his hands over both eyes so he could not see what was going on. I realize the difficulty of the financial critic of the Tory party. He had a terribly hard time finding any justification for criticizing the budget, but he did the best he could under the circumstances.

speechtext:
In the year 1946 when our present Minister of Finance took over, you will recall what I said to him. I told the minister at that time that he should roll up his sleeves and get down to work to see what made the clock tick rather than listen to his financial advisers. Well, Mr. Abbott did that, and I shall show you the record. In 1947, he reduced Canada's national debt by $373,648,000. In 1948 he reduced Canada's debt by $676,119,000. Would the financial critic of the Conservative party say that was wrong? No. In 1949, he reduced it by $595,502,000. Would he say that was wrong? In 1950, he reduced it again by $131,525,000. Would he say that was wrong? Then again in 1951, he reduced it by $211,294,000. If the country had been going behind as it was under the Tory regime from 1930 to 1935, we would have been paying an extra $62 million per year in interest.
I realize that the position of the opposition is a difficult one. They hate to sit back and see the progress and expansion the country is experiencing with the Liberals in the driver's seat. No country in the world has such a record and such a continuous excellent-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this budget presented to parliament on April 8, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) estimated that he would have a surplus of $9 million at the end of the present fiscal year. To anyone who has studied this budget; who has studied conditions in the country today; and who is familiar with this government's method of producing tax reductions in an election year, there is not the slightest doubt that we will end up this year with a surplus at least as great as the one we had at the end of the year just past.
My reasons for saying that are twofold.
First of all, the basic tax rates this year are substantially the same as they were a year ago. Income tax rates are up, and some commodity taxes are down.
Secondly, our gross national production, our gross national income, and our consumer spending, upon which all taxes are levied, are expected to be substantially greater this year than they were last year. I therefore

The Budget-Mr. Hees feel that we may expect tax revenues this year to be considerably above 1951; enough to more than take care of our increased defence expenditure.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, when the minister presented his budget on April 8 he said, as recorded on page 1250 of Hansard:
In line with past experience, I expect there will be a shortfall of expenditures below the amount provided by parliament in the appropriation votes.
Therefore, I believe that we can expect approximately the same budget surplus at the end of this year as we had at the end of the year just past. I believe that this fact makes it necessary for us to ask ourselves several questions.
First of all, why does this government find it necessary to overtax the people this year so that it can have a surplus at the end of the fiscal year?
The second question is, is it because next year, 1953, will be an election year, and the government will then be able to make substantial tax reductions, and so attempt to win votes for the Liberal party? What the government is actually doing is taking money out of the people's pockets this year so that they can pay it back to them next year.
In short, under the present government, we have in this country a budgetary system which estimates a surplus of $9 million, but which, in its very structure, provides for revenues in excess of expenditures, which admittedly will fall far short of the requested appropriation votes.
I believe that no reasonably minded Canadian objects to paying taxes necessary to pay for the cost of defence, both at home and in co-operation with our allies abroad. Nor do I believe that reasonably minded Canadians object to bearing the cost of necessary social security measures. However, to implement in this country a budgetary system which overestimates expenditures, and underestimates revenues, resulting in unjust and unwarranted taxation, would constitute in my mind a political fraud which should not be condoned in any democratic country.
In the pre-election budget of 1949, the government announced sweeping tax reductions amounting to $369 million in that year. While the obvious reason for this change of heart by the government in its 1949 budget was the impending general election, the reasons given parliament were as follows: First, that the increasing flow of goods available for sale to consumers, without higher prices, made these reductions economically feasible;
Second, the expected surplus of revenue over expenditure;
[Mr. Hees.J

Third, the reduction of $1,600 million made in the public debt since the war;
And fourth, the government felt that most Canadians would support, and even welcome, enlarged measures of tax reduction.
If these reasons for sweeping tax reductions in the pre-election budget of 1949 were valid, then surely they warrant consideration now, when:
First of all, consumer goods are not only available but are stockpiled in clogged inventories;
Second, when revenues will most surely exceed expenditures for the reasons I have given;
Third, when the amount paid off the national debt stands at $2,344 million as against $1,600 million in 1949;
And fourth, because there can be no doubt that the Canadian people would welcome relief from the present excessive and unwarranted high levels of taxation.
I believe that in the light of present conditions, and the relationship which these conditions bear to the government's action in its pre-election budget of 1949, a cyclical budgetary system, governed by elections and political expediency, is unwarranted, is fraudulent, is an affront to parliament, and should be discarded immediately.
Several weeks before this budget was presented to parliament, the house voted unanimously to do away with the four per cent limit on medical expenses as a deductible expense for income tax puposes. There was not one single dissenting voice in this house. However, despite this unanimous voice of parliament, the minister, in his budget address, said that he did not believe that the four per cent limit should be done away with, and so he completely nullified the unanimous voice of parliament.

speechtext:
You have no choice in the matter.
Mr. Nose worthy: I do not want to give the impression that this group does not agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw to the extent that there is need for careful scrutinizing of government expenditures and the expenditure of many departments of the government. I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw was correct when he said that no private business that approximated to any extent the size of the business that is carried' on by the government today would be carried on by the methods followed by the government.
His suggestion that there should be a central purchasing agency, and that there should be a committee of this house set up for the express purpose of scrutinizing government expenditures, as is done in the United States and elsewhere, are suggestions that most members in this house will agree with. At a time when federal, provincial and municipal taxes are taking 33 per cent of our national income, I suggest it does behoove us to scrutinize carefully where there is waste, or where the public is not getting value for the dollars that are collected and- spent.
Why I rose was to support the subamendment which was moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on April 22, and1 which is found on page 1489 of Hansard as follows:
This house further regrets that the government has ignored the wish of this house, as expressed by a unanimous vote on March 26, that the four per cent floor under medical expenses deductible for income tax purposes should be abolished.
55704-100i
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
I rise to support that subamendment with a full knowledge of the utter futility of opposition criticism in this house. My experience in this house has been that, constituted as the house is, opposition criticism is absolutely futile. The government just does not condescend to accept, or pay the slightest attention to any criticism that may come from this side of the house, no matter how well founded that criticism may be. I shall give examples of that at a later time.
I think the wish of the house in the unanimous acceptance it gave to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on March 26, and to which reference is made in the subamendment, was made quite clear. I do not think there is any doubt on the part of any member that Liberals and opposition members alike wanted not merely consideration of that question, but to have the four per cent floor removed. I do not think there is any doubt about it. I do not think Liberal members who gave their consent to that resolution wanted a mere consideration, without themselves feeling strongly one way or another as to whether the government should accept the resolution, after giving it consideration.
The country feels today that that four per cent floor should be removed. And when the house voted on the resolution, which was worded in the only way in which it could possibly be presented to the house, it expressed its desire to the minister, and indicated that it wanted the four per cent floor removed.
But after giving consideration, the minister chose to ignore the wishes of parliament. That is the point at issue here. The house has no authority to go farther than to recommend for the consideration of the minister any matter affecting the spending of public money. The house gave the minister its opinion in the only way that opinion could be given, and that applied not only to opposition members but also to Liberals.
I am confident that hon. members sitting on the government benches were just as serious in their desire to have the four per cent floor removed as were our members in the opposition. But what happened? We got not the slightest attention to our request; and this would seem to indicate that in this country we have reached a situation where we no longer have government by parliament, but rather government by a cabinet, or by individual members of that cabinet.
After all, I presume members are elected for some purpose. We are sent here to express as well as we can to the government our wishes in respect of legislation coming before the house. We are here to interpret to
1580	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy the government, so far as we can, the wishes of the people we represent. But in this parliament we have reached the stage where such representations are simply ignored.
No matter how we try, even when Liberal members join with the opposition in trying to impress upon a cabinet minister what they believe the country wants, that cabinet minister can afford to ignore those wishes. I suppose it is too much to expect a Liberal member to oppose a cabinet minister's policy on the floor of the house. There was a time when that was done. I sat in an earlier parliament in which there were any number of Liberal members who were quite ready to stand in their places in the house and criticize policies set forth by the cabinet. But we do not get much of that today. Surely it must be possible for those Liberal members who do not feel free to express opposition to cabinet policy when it is set forth in the house to express such opposition in their own caucuses. I just cannot understand a situation in which every Liberal member in the house on the occasion of the passage of a resolution gives his support to that resolution, and yet will sit in caucus with a minister and permit him to ignore completely the wishes set forth by Liberal and opposition members alike. I should think that, regardless of what Liberal members may do in the house, surely they must be able to influence government policy in their own caucuses.
I certainly hope that, while the minister has indicated in his budget that the four per cent floor is to remain, those Liberal members who supported the resolution in the house will make it quite clear to the minister that they want to have adopted the opinion expressed in the vote on the resolution.
The minister set forth certain objections to eliminating the four per cent floor. He pointed out that originally the legislation was intended to give relief only in exceptional or extraordinary cases of illness. Whatever may have been the original intention of the legislation, the intention of members in the house was quite implicit in the resolution that, regardless of the original intention, we now wanted to have the four per cent floor removed. And, after all, who is to determine what would be considered extraordinary expenses in a case of this kind?
Surely there are tens of thousands of people to whom a hospital bill of $100 is just as great a hardship as a bill of $1,000 or $2,000 to some other citizens. I do not ithink the minister or anyone else can say that a hospital bill of $100 is just an ordinary affair, and that that is not the kind of burden to which the legislation was intended to apply. The fact remains
IMr. Noseworthy.]

that this house and the taxpayers of this country, the people who are directly affected by this, expected that when the resolution passed this house it would be implemented in the budget.
The minister's assistant raises the objection that there would be administrative difficulty in checking hospital and medical bills, but I would draw his attention to what is done in the case of donations for charitable purposes. There must be tens of thousands of citizens whose charitable donations are comparatively small, who give $1, $2, or $5 to the Red Cross during its annual drive and who deduct that amount from their taxable income. If it can be done in the one instance, I fail to see why it cannot be done in the other.
There is another instance in which the minister's action is in direct opposition to the wishes of parliament as expressed in the resolution to which I have referred. The minister retained the four per cent floor but he raised the ceiling. My contention is that that raising of the ceiling will not benefit the class of people about whom we were concerned when we asked for consideration of the abolition of the four per cent floor. The raising of the ceiling to $2,000 will benefit the wealthier citizens who can afford to go to the more expensive hospitals and hire the more expensive specialists, but a $2,000 hospital or sickness bill is something that the ordinary workingman just could not contemplate because it would ruin him. The working people of this country are not the ones who are going to benefit by the raising of that ceiling, but it was those people with whom the house was concerned when we asked for consideration of the removal of the floor of four per cent.
I want to turn for a moment to the question of the personal income tax and the budget and discuss the minister's alleged reduction of six per cent in the personal income tax. In my opinion the minister sought to take credit for an actual reduction in income tax. It is true that his statement on page 1254 of Hansard is quite explicit, and in order to be fair to the minister I shall read it. He said:
In other words, the average taxpayer will pay six per cent less than he would otherwise have done under the income tax law as it now stands.
The interpretation which the country took from that statement was that there would be an actual lowering of the income tax this year. I think the minister contributed to that impression when he said, as reported on page 1255:
I think I should make clear that the reductions in income tax which I have announced will not be sufficient, for most taxpayers, to offset the effect of the old age security tax.

In other words he sought to show the Canadian taxpayer that if by chance he found his 1952 taxes actually higher than his 1951 taxes, the fault lay with the social security tax. The minister succeeded to some extent in spreading that impression throughout the country. For instance, the U. S. News and World Report of April 18, page 82, had this to say:
Canada's personal income tax is being reduced by 6 per cent. For low-income taxpayers, most of the benefit of that cut will be wiped out by a new social security tax that takes effect July 1.
Our own wide-awake Canadian journalists were not slow in seeing through the so-called tax reduction. In the issue of April 26 the editor of Saturday Night stated the case quite clearly when he said:
No one can say that this year's budget was straightforward. The general public must have realized by now that what Mr. Abbott called reductions in income tax are increases over what we paid last year even before you add the social security tax.
That is the actual situation. One would naturally expect that when the minister announced that there was going to be a six per cent reduction in personal income tax this year the man with $2,000 taxable income would pay less in 1952 than he paid in 1951. That is the meaning which ordinary people took out of the statement that taxes were to be reduced six per cent. The actual fact is that even before the two per cent-this year one per cent-social security tax is added the taxpayer actually will pay more in 1952 on the same taxable income than he paid in 1951. A single person whose income was $1,800 in 1951 paid $132 taxes; in 1952, before adding the social security tax, he will pay $140, an increase of $8. A single person with an income of $2,000 paid $165 in 1951. In 1952, before the social security tax is added, he will pay $175, an increase of $10. A man with an income of $5,000 paid $770 in 1951. The same man with the same income will pay $820 in 1952 before the social security tax is added, an increase in 1952 over 1951 of $50. It is not surprising that one of our humorous writers

I think it was Bruce West in the Toronto Globe and Mail-wrote an article on the minister's tax reduction and suggested that since the minister by reducing taxes this year is making us pay more taxes then possibly next year he should increase taxes so that we may be paying less. It is quite possible that the skilled magician who is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) could by a sleight-of-hand trick convince us next year that by increasing taxes he is actually going to reduce them just as this year while supposedly reducing taxes he actually increased them.
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
I want to deal for a moment with the sales tax. In his budget speech the minister said that in his opinion the sales tax is a fair levy. We believe, and have so stated in the house on many occasions, that even with the exemptions from the sales tax it still bears most heavily on those who are least able to pay. The sales tax ignores one of the basic principles of good taxation. It ignores entirely the principle of taxation according to the ability of the person taxed to pay that tax. I should like to remind the house and the minister that all-told the sales and excise taxes now produce about 30 per cent of Canada's federal income. In the United States, where they have sales taxes and to some extent excise taxes, they raise only
11	per cent of their federal budget by these two means. We have maintained and still maintain that the sales tax is not a good tax, that it is a hidden tax, and that the people in the lower income groups, the people with large families to raise, suffer most from that tax.
On the question of corporation taxes the minister expressed regret that they could not be substantially reduced this year but he held out some hope to the corporations that that result might be achieved in future years. The opinion expressed by the minister was shared by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the financial critic of the official opposition. Unfortunately, and here I think I can speak for this group, we do not share that concern. I do not feel that the corporations have suffered to any great extent by being overburdened with taxation during the past year. In his budget speech the minister indicated that his own estimate of corporation profits made a year ago was
12	per cent too low, that corporation profits for the year 1950 were 12 per cent higher than the minister estimated in April of 1951.
The minister also indicated that much of his surplus resulted from the fact that he underestimated corporation profits. That would suggest to me at least that these corporations have not suffered by being overtaxed. I notice that the minister estimates an increase of $13 million in corporation taxes for the coming year. If his estimate is as conservative as it was last year, then it is quite evident that the minister expects corporation profits to continue to increase this year as they have been doing every year since the war. Here again I should like to make a comparison between Canada and the United States by reference to the publication to which I have already referred. At page 84 there is the following:
Corporations, like individuals, are to get a slight reduction in tax rates under the new Canadian budget.

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
Here I might interject that I sincerely hope the proposed reduction in corporation taxes will not work out the same as the reduction in personal income tax. The writer goes on to say:
The result will be that, so far as the central government in Canada is concerned, the top effective tax rate on corporations will be 45 per cent. In addition, there are provincial taxes of 5 to 7 per cent. Canada has no excess profits tax, and the new budget proposes none. In the United States corporations pay a regular federal tax of 52 per cent, plus an excess profits tax of 30 per cent. The average federal tax is about 60 per cent. On top of that, 32 states impose relatively small taxes. So the Canadian corporation, by comparison, comes off fairly easily.
The concern expressed by the minister for corporations is not too well founded, and certainly is not shared by this group.
Turning now to the excise tax reductions, I want to say that we welcome such reductions as the minister saw fit to make, particularly in the taxes that were imposed a year ago. Certainly there was a crying need for those reductions. If the reductions did nothing else they showed that the minister is now willing to acknowledge that he made a mistake a year ago in imposing those taxes. Speaker after speaker from all opposition groups tried to point out to the minister when these taxes were being imposed that he was going to injure our economy. Speaker after speaker tried to persuade the minister not to impose those taxes. The budget speech bears witness to the fact that the opposition members were right and the minister was wrong. During the past year those taxes caused pockets of unemployment and brought unnecessary hardship to thousands of Canadian citizens. The minister gives those taxes some credit for halting inflation. Our position, and I think that of all three opposition groups in the house last year, was that these were not the best measures to curb inflation, that other things could be done which would be much less harmful to the Canadian public.
I wanted to say a word or two on the surplus, about which we have heard so much. I suppose the great conundrum arising out of the budget is when a surplus is not a surplus. The big question is just what was the surplus last year. Was it $1,009 million? Was it $722 million? Or was it a mere $356 million? In the government's monthly report at the end of December an interim surplus of $722 million was shown. Then in the budget the minister tells us that he made certain non-budgetary cash outlays from the surplus which totalled $653 million, and that after making those outlays he still bad a surplus of $356 million. Well, $356 million plus $653 million paid out in non-budgetary cash outlays totals $1,009 million. So the country is left with the big question: just how large was


the actual surplus? Apparently the minister had to do as much juggling with his surplus as he did with the personal income tax.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think we can agree with hon. members who have already indicated that this budget favours the rich to the disadvantage of the poor. While the hon. member for Greenwood did not express that opinion in those words, he came very close to it; and when the official critic of the Progressive Conservative party feels that a budget is benefiting the well to do at the expense of those in the lower income brackets, I am convinced there must be something in his statement. As a matter of fact the effect of the income tax was very well shown by the hon. member when he pointed out the disparity in the increase this year between those in the lower income groups and those in the higher income groups. That can be found at page 1478 of Hansard. In the distribution of the social security tax, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) at page 1485 of Hansard, we have another example. The sales tax, which bears most heavily upon those in the lower income groups, is to contribute $135 million toward the cost of social security; personal income tax is to contribute $52 million; and the corporation tax $48 million. The fact that some slight relief was given corporations while there was no reduction whatever in the sales tax is one more indication that this government has been getting closer and closer to St. James street and farther and farther away from the common people of this country. The high percentage of the federal revenue raised by sales and personal income taxes indicates that disregard for the interests of the common people and illustrates the lack of sympathy on the part of this government for those in the ordinary walks of life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to experts in different lines of business make their contributions to this debate, I almost hesitate to take part in it. Just an hour or so ago we heard quite an address on high finance. I am afraid many of us were not able to take in everything the speaker said, and will have to be enlightened further as the days go by.
This evening I do not intend to give the budget any new name. It has been called so many uncomplimentary things that I do not think it needs another name. It has been very well described by the speakers who have preceded me. Many people were keeping their fingers crossed until April 8 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) delivered his budget. Many people hesitated to buy things such as automobiles and other necessary equipment, feeling that some reduction

in taxes would be made. In- particular, many people all across the country were hoping against hope for a reduction in the income tax levies. Taxation, of course, is just one of the headaches that the people have been suffering from for eleven or twelve years.
We have been paying exceedingly heavy income taxes. When the war ceased people thought that they would be granted some relief from the high levies of 1945, but we found we had to prepare for another defensive war. Some people call it policing, but after all it is actual war. The people did- not even have a short breathing spell until heavier taxes were again levied. As a result of the preparations for this defensive war which have been going on for some time we have drifted into a false state of prosperity about which the supporters of the present government are boasting, perhaps for political reasons and because of the expected election in 1953. But when people have to point to war, whether all-out or defensive, as a means of bringing about prosperity, then I think they should get off their high-horse and get back to sound thinking about peacetime prosperity an-d peacetime living. They should not be boosting the policies of their government.
As a result of this false prosperity we have a shortage of building material. Many of our men and women across the country, and the city of Ottawa is no exception, -are suffering from a shortage of houses. They are suffering from a shortage of -cash and credit by means of which they could provide themselves with these houses. We find that within the last day or -two even in this -city some of the -officials have been asking the service clubs to take the lead in providing houses. I believe that conditions are becoming very poor when such events occur. On the 6th of this month I listened -to a sermon by the minister of St. John's church in which he described very well what is happening today. Had he gone all the way and said what he should have said on that occasion perhaps he would have offended some of his parishioners who are supporters of this government, but he did say that because of the shortage of houses families of five or six people were compelled to live in one room. In many cases six, seven or eight families are compelled to use one bathroom. In my opinion such conditions should not exist. Had the government looked after its business as well as it has looked after some other things, such conditions would not occur.
Even after all these events, on the 17th of last month we found that we still had 337,000 unemployed. This is something of which the country should not be very proud. As I stated a moment ago, there are people who still want homes and many other things,
The Budget-Mr. Fair
yet we have this number of unemployed and some unused materials. In addition to these hardships, in the budget brought down by the minister on April 8, we have some added crippling taxation. The minister thought he would give us some good news and led the people to believe that there would be a decrease of six per cent in personal income taxes. Of course, that is not true. Without going to the trouble of preparing a set of figures of my own, I shall read once again the figures put on the record by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) on Tuesday last. I -think it is a good thing for the members to realize what is happening. These figures can be found on page 1490 of Hansard for April 22, 1952. The hon. member said:
Let us take into consideration married persons without children, those in that category. If the taxable income-that is, after the deduction of their $2,000 exemption-is $250, the 1951 tax is shown as $42; the 1952 tax is $44 plus the old age security levy of $2.50. This is an increase of $4.50 and a percentage increase of 10-7/10 per cent. If the taxable income is $1,000, the 1951 tax was $165; the 1952 tax, $175; the old age security levy, $10. The increase in 1952 over 1951 is $20, and that is a percentage increase of 12-1/10 per cent. If the taxable income is $3,000, then the 1951 tax was $561; the 1952 tax, $596, the old age security levy, $30; the increase in 1952 over 1951 is $65 or 11-6 per cent increase. If the taxable income is $8,000, the tax for 1951 was $1,826; the 1952 tax, $1,946; the old age security levy is $30, which is the ceiling for the old age security levy this year. That is an increase of $150 for 1952 over 1951, which would be a percentage increase of 8-2 per cent. Then if you jump up to the $98,000 taxable income category, $58,370 was the 1951 tax; the 1952 tax will be $61,220; the old age security levy, $30. The total increase for 1952 over 1951 would be $2,820 or a 4-9/10 per cent increase.
I do not need to go further, Mr. Speaker, because the figures I have given will show that instead of a policy of soaking the rich, which is advocated by some people, the policy of the Minister of Finance is to soak the poor, the people who can least afford to pay.
Turning to some of the o-ther taxes, we have the excise tax which was increased last year from 15 to 25 per cent on -certain commodities. In this year's budget it was put back to the original 15 per cent. In my opinion that tax should never have been levied. This opinion was expressed on many occasions during the discussion of the 1951 budget, but the minister would not make the required -changes. Figures which I placed on -the record on March 7 last when I spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne show that production of certain commodities has decreased, and the minister collected much less revenue than he would have collected if the tax had not been levied. In addition to that, unemployment increased and as a result of the unemployment many families had to go without things that their

The Budget-Mr. Fair
unemployed breadwinner should have been able to supply. We are wondering whether these tax reductions will be passed on to the consumer. Many people say they are not and from the prices quoted for different commodities I believe they have not been passed on. I wonder what the government is doing in this connection. If the benefits of the tax cut are not being passed on, then I believe that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) some weeks ago should be adopted; that is, that the government should cut the tariff on many of the goods that are bearing a high tariff today, and let our manufacturers bring their profits down to some extent as well as passing on the benefits to the consumer.
Some mention was made of the drop in the cost-of-living index. Here again let me point out that according to an article in the Ottawa Journal of April 4 under the heading: "Mostly due to meat price cuts." the decrease in the cost-of-living index was due to decrease in the price of farm products. This is what the editorial said:
Index shows decline for second consecutive month.
The cost-of-living index during February declined by 1-7 points to 189 1 from 190-8, the bureau of statistics reported today.
The second consecutive monthly decline in the prices barometer, based on 1935-39 prices equalling 100, was sparked mostly by a drop in meat prices, the bureau said.
It was the biggest drop since December, 1942, when the index also declined by 1-7 points. The February decline followed a drop of seven-tenths of a point during January.
Meats declined along with eggs, oranges, cabbages, topcoats and men's suits. These overbalanced increases for rent, furniture, dishes, hardware, floor coverings, telephone rates in eastern Canada, domestic coal and health and personal care, along with newspapers and theatre admissions.
I am bringing this in for the purpose of showing that we are getting a cut in the cost of living at the expense of our people on the farms. You will find that practically all of the items that have been reduced are products of the farm; while those that have been increased are products of secondary industry. I feel that government policy at the present time is stacked against the farmer. Farm prices come down, while the cost of the goods the farmer has to buy in order to produce continually climb. We have, for instance, the international wheat agreement. In connection with that, when the first speaker after eight o'clock was on his feet, somebody across the way butted in with the remark of $65 million paid to the wheat growers of the west. I want to tell those who are interested in that question that in addition to the $65 million paid to the farmers they had a net loss of no less than $504 million on the British wheat agreement and on the cheap wheat supplied so that Canadians could eat cheap

bread during the 1946-49 crop years. As a result of the international wheat agreement and cheap bread still being provided to our Canadian consumers, further losses are continuing. One of these days I intend to put these on the record.
While the prices of everything that the farmer has to buy are increasing, we find that provision is made in the international wheat agreement, which will conclude at the end of July, 1953, for the floor price to drop 10 cents per bushel per year, and there is a constant top price of $1.80. At the present time, as all hon. members are aware, or should be aware, the Canadian consumers are eating bread baked from wheat sold to the Canadian millers at the same price as that sold under the international wheat agreement. Why that should be I cannot understand. Government policy, however, is to continue that program, and they have not given any justification for that.
In connection with the new international wheat agreement that is being negotiated in London at the present time, I am not sure whether it will be in the interests of our farmers unless a proposal somewhat similar to that which was put forward by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when the original international wheat agreement was being discussed is made use of. It will be noted that at that time there was the ceiling price and a decreasing floor price placed on our wheat without for one moment taking into consideration the price of the things that the farmer has to buy in order to produce that wheat. The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Acadia and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that it was impossible to find any method by which it could be done, the hon. member for Acadia pointed out to him that the international monetary fund had all of the figures required upon which to base a reasonable agreement.
The policy of supplying cheap wheat to our Canadian people all across the country is one other method of picking the pockets of the Canadian wheat growers, and only the prairie wheat growers, some 232,000 of them, during recent years. Then we have the price of beef. Some people are complaining about that. While the price of good cattle is fixed today at 25 cents at Toronto, that is 3J cents 'below the proposal made by the farm organizations of western Canada. It must be remembered that during recent months many people who are today feeding these cattle paid from 30 cents to 33 cents a pound for them. In addition to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease we have this other disaster of a drastic cut in prices, which will

discourage the feeding of these cattle in the future. People perhaps realize that they never miss the water until the well runs dry. You will never realize the injustice you are doing to the producers of livestock until you run short of meat, and then you will suddenly wake up and find out.
The floor price for pork is fixed at $26 at Toronto and Montreal and $24.50 at Winnipeg, but that is nothing to brag about in comparison with the cost of raising hogs at the present time. In my opinion it should have been $28 per hundred, and provision made, which is not made today, for compelling the packers to pay on the basis of the price set by the government.
Then, again, in the case of butter we have a floor price which is guaranteed only to the parties who pack that butter, and the producer is left out in the cold and at the mercy of the purchasers of his commodity. In the case of eggs there is a floor of 38 cents a dozen. Again that is not being paid to the producer, but is a guarantee only to the parties who pack them and have them at the end of the egg season.
For many weeks we have had the cheese producers coming to the government with their plea, with their briefs, to have something done about a floor price for cheese; but up to the present time nothing whatever has been done. Only on Monday we had a question asked of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his reply was that they were watching the situation, or words to that effect. I feel sure that some ways could be devised to provide prices which would benefit the producer rather than the other parties, namely the packers and others in that line of business.
Many of our daily papers are helping to continue to deceive the people of Canada with regard to our agricultural industry. I am glad that we have some weekly newspapers published in farming districts that have a much better grasp of the situation and that are willing to learn things from firsthand experience. Of course those fellows behind the desks in the city editorial rooms would not even think of studying agriculture. That is much too easy at the present time. Perhaps it is like what the banking industry used to be some time ago. Many people felt that if there was a dumb member of the family they had to put him on the farm in order that he could make a living, but today we find in editorial chairs, in the banks, and in other places, many of those dumb members of families. They are placed there so that they can make 55704-101
The Budget-Mr. Fair
a living. That will explain the reasons for some of the stupid editorials we see in our newspapers.
I have here, however, an editorial from the Wainwright Star-Chronicle, which is a weekly newspaper, and a very useful one, printed in my constituency. It has been circulated for a number of years. Some time ago when people were discussing the butter question, and the high prices paid for butter, this editorial appeared:
Some of our daily publications seem to be rather badly troubled about the farmer getting too much money for his butter, and failing to co-operate with his market, the consumer, in providing an adequate supply of this product. Sometimes we think it might be a good idea if those who protest that the farmer or the dairyman is making money too easily were required to do a stint of duty on the farm. While we must admit that the price of livestock has been very satisfactory of late-
And I might add that this was written before the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth disease was made known.
-and dairy products prices have been at a more satisfactory level, we feel that until prices for farm products are such that the farmer can work a forty-hour week and can pay something approaching union scale wages to his help for a union week, we have not been called upon to give the farmer a much greater reward for his effort than is his due.
It appears to us that there are a lot of other trades which have upped their prices quite a lot more than the farmers, and who, if and when they wish, practise "scarcity" marketing.
We're all behind the farmer.
I might say that the purpose of many people being behind the farmer is so that they can boot him good and hard.
He works so hard, he works so long and he gets so little, may be somewhat of an exaggeration, but there is no doubt that when one considers the amount of work he does, the extreme uncertainty of his cash rewards, and the ever growing cost of operation, he is not the most overpaid citizen in Alberta.
Only this morning I noticed in the Ottawa Citizen that authority has been given to the steel producers in the United States to increase their price to the extent of $3 per ton. We import large quantities of steel from that country, and I would expect that in the very near future we will have another increase in the price of farm machinery.
When I spoke in the debate on the address in reply, on March 7, I advocated that something be done about setting up a royal commission to investigate farm machinery prices. Away back in 1937 or 1938 a similar investigation was held in the House of Commons, and the figures brought out at that time showed that almost 70 per cent of the machinery manufactured in Canada went to the farmers of the west. So that when the statement was made some time ago by a member of the house that the west was

opened up for the benefit of central Canada, I suggest it was a correct statement, and that its truth is proved by those figures.
In my opinion farm machinery prices today are much too high, and in a moment or two I hope to place upon the record figures showing those prices. Apparently farm machinery manufacturers feel that the goose is laying the golden egg, and at least some of them are not allowing their agents to cash in on the increased prices. Some time ago a percentage was paid, but I understand that at the moment the agent collects a stipulated amount for each unit sale he makes. Those commissions have not kept pace with recent price increases. Many of them are protesting, and I should not be surprised if in the near future some action were taken by those agents.
In the Alberta wheat pool budget, under the heading, "The Cost of Farming", we find some interesting information. This is the issue of April 11, 1952, only a short time ago. It states:
The cost of goods and services used by farmers in western Canada is considerably more than double that of the prewar years. In January the index figure stood at 223-5. By way of comparison, the cost of living index for all of Canada that month was 191-5. In both cases the base period of 1935-39 equals 100.
The index of commodities and services used by farmers in western Canada, and farm living costs, during the month of January was reported by the dominion bureau of statistics as follows:
Index number
Composite index, excluding living costs 227-3
Equipment and materials	 217-3
Farm machinery	 196-4
Building materials	 332-5
Gasoline, oil and grease	 137-8
Feed	 252-6
Fertilizer	 161-8
Binder twine	 448-3
I might say that one of the dealers told me recently that the price of binder twine would be up another $4 per hundredweight for the 1952 crop year. Then it continues:

Seed	 248-7
Hardware	 208-8
Taxes and interest rates	 159-7
Farm wages	 382-4
Let me say that that is one of the items of farm expense that should have been increased, because farm workers were working at wages far below what they should have been receiving, when compared with the wages paid in other industries. Then it continues:
Index number
Farm family living costs	 217-8
