Those figures should suffice to show that farming costs have increased drastically, 

while the prices of products the farmer sells -have been static or, in many cases, reduced during recent months. I am not going to say more about agriculture at the present time, because I have only a limited time at my disposal.
There is one other matter however about which I should like to speak. I am referring to the physically incapacitated persons in Canada. I felt that at this session we would have an opportunity to discuss this matter, because at the opening of the session I believe the second item on the list of notices of motions was one in the name of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial governments for the purpose of providing pensions, equal to old age pensions, for all those who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
I was surprised to note that, for some mysterious reason, the resolution was dropped. Then during the last day or so, we find a resolution worded in exactly the same way appearing almost at the bottom of the list of notices of motion. I would expect -therefore that we would not be able to have an opportunity to discuss the motion or to have a vote upon it at the present session.
On many occasions during the last few years inquiries have been made as to what the government intended to do for those who are incapacitated. Up to the present time we have not had much satisfaction. The hon. member for Fort William did make his speech in the budget debate a couple of days ago, upon which occasion he made reference to physically incapacitated persons, and brought out many good points with which I could heartily agree. The only trouble however is that in spite of all the praise he has given each and every cabinet minister who comes before the house, we have not yet received from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) any legislation to provide those pensions so sincerely sought by so many members in the house. I am surprised that these pensions have not been provided for. I understand that last year we had a national production of $21,200 million and we also had a surplus of several hundred million dollars. On April 15 the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) spoke to -the Western Ontario Liberal Association, and I quote from a report in the Ottawa Citizen of April 16, as follows:
Although taxes are unusually high for a peacetime budget, people of Canada never were better off and prosperity is at its highest peak, Hon. Paul Martin, Minister of Health and Welfare, said Monday.

Speaking before the annual meeting of the Western Ontario Liberal Association, he said the government was faced with the "grave situation of preparing a defence system for Canada and had no alternative but to keep taxes high.
Freedom must be bought and this country is spending two billion dollars this year to see Canadians remain free."
Despite the heavy levy, Mr. Martin said Canadians and the nation never were so prosperous.
If we are so prosperous, why in the world does not the government put into effect a pension policy for those who are unable to help themselves? Is there a deliberate holding up of this legislation until perhaps next year when many of us expect an election and when it can be used as another bribe to get votes so that the government can be returned to power? The minister continued:
Labour income and investment is at a record high and on a per capita basis Canada leads the world in international trade.
Perhaps if the people of Canada had the means with which to purchase their requirements we would not have so much for export. Much of the exports about which the Minister of National Health and Welfare was boasting are being made to our potential enemies in the form of bullets and other things that go with a war, defensive or otherwise. The minister went on:
Canada has been referred to in world circles as being the land of great promise and excellent government.
< Perhaps that should have been changed a little bit so as to read: "Canada has been referred to in world circles as being an excellent country with a government of great promises".
As one example of this, the Minister of Finance promised Canadians a decrease of six per cent in their income tax whereas we find in fact these taxes will be increased from eight to twelve per cent in the low income brackets. That is not good enough. I think the people of Canada are wakening up to what is happening.
The world at large is in need of greater food production and we have the potential means of producing food in great abundance. But when you speak to farmers about this many say, "What is the use? If we produce more crops there are no markets for them and even if we do get a chance to sell our products the government comes along with its income tax legislation and takes our money. So why bother?"
If we had a financial policy that would work in the interests of the common people, that would make it possible for every family to have a decent home and enjoy a decent standard of living, then I think we would have much greater production than we have at the present time. There would be less 55704-101J
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith need for worry and war. Social credit can provide that policy if the government will only make use of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I want first to compliment the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) upon the address he made this evening and the courage he displayed. I do not agree with everything he had to say, but I think it was an honest speech. If there were more members in this house with the courage of the hon. member for Moose Jaw I think it would be of benefit to parliament. I have often wondered where we would be heading if a socialist government was elected in Canada, but if we had the hon. member for Moose Jaw as the Minister of Finance possibly they would not put us altogether on the rocks.
I have a few matters to deal with, but first I should like to refer to the budget. Many things have been said about the budget and while I think there is in it really nothing to cheer about, at the same time there is nothing to cry about. I think the people of Canada got pretty well what they expected from the budget. Speaking for the people of my constituency, I think it is just about what they expected. I think Canadians generally realize that you cannot play both ends against the middle. If you are going to have additional services, public works and so on, you must have high taxes. The hon. member for Moose Jaw pointed that out very clearly.
Many illustrations have been given since this debate began of just what this budget means to the Canadian taxpayer. I am going to repeat an illustration which has been used on two occasions by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance is reported on page 1526 of Hansard of April 23 as having said:
I shall use the example the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar used yesterday, the simple case of the married man with an income of $3,000. He has an exemption of $2,000. His first $1,000 of taxable income in 1950 was taxed at the rate of 15 per cent, and in 1950 he paid $150.
And again:
Therefore while in 1950 he paid $150, he paid $165 in 1951.
That individual had an increase of $15 per year in his income tax. Let us assume that that man is going to buy a small automobile. As a result of the budget, he will save $150 because of the reduced taxes on that automobile. If he were to buy an electric stove he would save $50 on the cheaper type. If he were to pay this additional $15 income

The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith tax for the next ten years he would save it on the purchase of one automobile.
I want at this time to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the decreases in the taxes on automobiles. When I spoke before the Easter recess I suggested that the taxes on automobiles should be eliminated entirely. This is a start, however, and as budgets go on in the future I hope that the taxes on automobiles will be eliminated entirely. I said at that time that I thought the automobile industry of Canada had grown up. I still think so, and if it were given a chance to stand on its own feet I think it could compete with that industry in other countries.
I want to refer to the price of farm machinery. The other day the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke about the prices of machinery in Canada and compared those prices with what the farmer gets for his products. He suggested that a committee or commission should be appointed to investigate the price of machinery. I agree with the hon. member, although I do not agree that we should start in where the Saskatchewan government left off. In Saskatchewan a committee was set up in February by the provincial government to investigate the price of farm machinery. I said publicly at the time in Saskatchewan that it was nothing but a smokescreen, a snowman that would melt in the March sun, and it has already done so. The reason it has done so is that even if there was a combine or cartel existing in the machinery industry there is not a province in the Dominion of Canada that could do anything about it.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to the fact that some of the companies would not give the Saskatchewan committee all the information they wanted. I am sure he was not surprised. Why should they? What could the provincial government do if they did find the price of machinery was too high? If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was sincere-and I am sure he was- I think he could have joined with me when less than six months ago I brought up the same subject in the house. He did not see fit to do so but I will join with him now. However, let us leave the Saskatchewan committee out of it. Personally I think it was only set up for political reasons and, as I stated before, it was only a snowman and has already melted. On October 19, 1951, in speaking in the house I referred to an address made the day before by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and I quoted a part of his speech. I


am going to quote it again. I said, as found at page 228 of Hansard for that date:
Let us see what the hon. member for Coast-Capilano had to say yesterday. As reported at page 162 of Hansard he said:
"I learned a good deal this summer about combines, cartels and monopolies-indeed this has been a very beneficial summer for me-at the United Nations. If there is one country in the world which has tried to wipe out cartels, combines and business monopolies, it has been the United States of America-and this goes away back to Teddy Roosevelt's time. The Americans have found that no matter how they attacked the problem of monopolies, combines and trusts in their own country, international cartels have to be attacked internationally. With that in mind they put forward a resolution before the United Nations to have an international commission which would deal internationally with cartels beyond the reach of any individual government. I, as the Canadian representative, was glad to second that resolution."
At that time I went on to say:
I have read that to the house to show that so far as machinery is concerned, if these things do exist within the machinery industry, there is nothing that this government can do alone, but it certainly can do something in co-operation with the United States.
Therefore I suggest that when the government of Saskatchewan set up their committee last February they must have known perfectly well that if there was anything wrong with the price of machinery there was nothing they could do about it. Nevertheless I will join with any member from any part of the house who urges the government- and I already have once-to investigate the machinery industry in Canada. However, I want to be fair. As farmers we have been complaining about the price of machinery rising since 1946. I have an article in my hand from the Winnipeg Free Press. I have also seen the same statement in Maclean's magazine and I have not heard or seen it refuted. The heading is, "Farm tools up only 66 per cent in ten years". The article reads:
The Increase in retail prices of other commodities since 1941 has far exceeded that of farm machinery, G. A. McMillan of Toronto, Canadian sales manager for Massey-Harris Company Limited, told the Free Press, Friday. In Winnipeg to confer with sales representatives for Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, Mr. McMillan said farm machinery prices have risen only 66 per cent in the ten-year period. But the cost of raw materials is up about 98 per cent and hourly wage rates had risen by 158 per cent. Mr. McMillan said the Massey-Harris Company had spent about $34 million-most of it in Canada-enlarging its operation since 1941. A $225,000 depot had been erected in Winnipeg.
I hold no brief for the machine companies but I want to be fair, and if that is the case -and I have not heard anyone refute it-then if they are making excess profits they certainly have not been making as much since 1946 up to the present time as they were prior to that. That is all I am going to say about farm machinery at the moment.

I want to speak for a few moments about the South Saskatchewan dam. At the outset I want to say that as far as I personally and the people of my constituency are concerned we will not benefit any more from the Saskatchewan dam than will the constituencies of Manitoba. I could use the constituency of Souris as an example. I think the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) will agree with me. I think he knows my constituency about as well as I know his, and I think his constituency will not benefit any more than mine. I hope that before too long we can get on with the job. I do not often quote editorials but I have one here to which I should like to refer. It is taken from a farm paper, the Western Producer of April 10, 1952. It deals with the debate that went on in the Saskatchewan legislature this winter with respect to the dam. It reads in part:
When the subject was debated in the Saskatchewan legislative assembly it seemed at times that anybody who dared to cast doubts on its soundness was regarded as no better than a traitor. The main thing appeared to be to get on with the job-start spending the money. Surely those who are convinced of the feasibility and soundness of the scheme should welcome full investigation. This is far too big a thing to monkey around with or with which to play petty politics.
I wholeheartedly agree with that statement. It continues:
Surely no one wants western agriculture to be saddled with a white elephant for which it will take generations to pay. On the other hand, if the practical value of the proposition is determined beyond reasonable doubt, no one need fear that it will be proceeded with against any opposition. It may be doubted whether the performances put on by those legislators in Regina who seemed more interested in playing politics than in building dams will be helpful.
Well, I hope we in this house will not play politics with that dam. Last fall the government decided to appoint a commission to take one more look at the project, but I do not believe it has been able to make a report as yet. I hope that may be done in the very near future. Within the last day or so, however, I have learned from very reliable sources that this commission is holding meetings in western Canada, one in Lethbridge and one in Winnipeg. I should like to know why a commission needs to go to Winnipeg or Lethbridge to decide whether it is feasible to build a dam in Saskatchewan.
I am sure that when the St. Mary's dam was being considered there were no meetings held in Saskatchewan to decide whether or not a dam should be built in Alberta. It may have been necessary for the commission to go to Saskatchewan to decide upon the feasibility of this undertaking. I would not object to that, but I do criticize it for this delay. To me that is a lot of nonsense, and I hope those
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith in the government who are looking after this matter will see that they get down to work and give us a report yes or no.
One other matter I want to mention briefly is the damp grain in western Canada. It is not too often that I give bouquets to the government on the floor of this house. I do that in my constituency, and very successfully, I may say. However, I want to tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that we appreciate the way this grain has been handled, and I think that goes for those hon. members who do not support the government. I understand the grain is being moved with very little danger of spoiling, and we do appreciate that very much.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The sun did
not help very much. In conclusion I want to refer again to redistribution, and what is going to happen in western Canada. When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) presented his bill I asked, for the information of those who were opposed to it, what could be done so that Saskatchewan would not lose five seats, 25 per cent of its representation. The Prime Minister looked at me with a smile and said it would be necessary to amend the constitution; that that was a big order, but it would be given consideration. Well, it has been given consideration, and it seems that we will lose three seats instead of five.
I want to tell the Prime Minister and members of the government that we greatly appreciate this consideration. The job may have been big but it looks as though it will be done. I think all hon. members from Saskatchewan, including the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and those of the C.C.F. party, will join me in thanking the Prime Minister. Perhaps I should go further and thank all hon. members, from the maritime provinces, the central provinces, Manitoba and British Columbia for their kind consideration in this regard.
That is all I have to say at this time, Mr. Speaker. No doubt there will be other opportunities to speak in this debate, though I do not believe I will do so unless I am provoked into it.
On motion of Mr. Tustin the debate was adjourned.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY   REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN TORONTO "STAR" OF APRIL 23
ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY   REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN TORONTO "STAR" OF APRIL 23
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker,
I wish to refer to a press clipping from the

Privilege-Mr. Chevrier Toronto Daily Star of April 23, 1952, which was brought to my attention late this afternoon. The heading is "Canada to push seaway, ignore U.S.-Chevrier." The body of the article goes on to say:
Ottawa, April 23-Canada is going to push ahead with her plans for the all-Canadian St. Lawrence seaway and joint Canadian-U.S. power project just as if the U.S. Senate wasn't considering U.S. participation in the seaway, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, Minister of Transport, said today.
He was commenting on developments in the U.S. capital, where a senate committee reported the project to the Senate but without giving it a priority rating for consideration.
"We are going to continue to press for a joint application to the international joint committee and if something does happen to make it possible for the U.S. to participate on the basis of the 1941 agreement we will be all set to proceed with that," Mr. Chevrier said.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I made no such statement as that attributed to me in, the title, and the statements carried in the body of the article are not fully accurate. When I was asked by the correspondent of the Star over the telephone for my comments on the decision of the foreign relations committee of the Senate of the United States to refer the long-debated 1941 agreement to the floor of that body, I stated that Canada was going to press forward as strongly as it could for the all-Canadian seaway and the joint Canadian-United States power project by cooperation with the United States in filing an
application to the international joint commission. I added that if meanwhile the United States congress approved of the 1941 agreement, Canada would be ready to proceed with the seaway on the basis of that agreement.
A headline such as this does me an injustice and the St. Lawrence waterway project a disservice. I have repeatedly taken the position both in and out of this house that the Canadian government favours the 1941 agreement but that it could not wait indefinitely. As an alternative it was developing the allCanadian seaway. I hasten to add that I am led to believe that the correspondent reporting this statement is not himself responsible for the heading of it, but that does not detract from the harm and injury a statement such as this could do, particularly if it got any circulation in the United States. For that reason I felt that a correction should be made without delay.
